sourceDefinition: Easy; applied to a pace. (M, K.) ― -b2- Easy in pace; applied to a he-camel: fem. with p : (S, M, K:) or soft, or gentle, in pace; applied to a he-camel and to a she-camel: (Msb:) and ↓ mirosaAlN , also, applied to a she-camel, has the former of these significations; and its pl. is maraAsiylu : (S, K:) or this pl. signifies light, or active, she-camels, that give thee what they have to give spontaneously; and rasolapN is applied to one thereof: a she-camel is termed ↓ mirosaAlN as being likened to the arrow thus called. (TA.) ― -b3- Soft, and lax, or flaccid: [app. applied to a he-camel; for it is added,] one says naAqapN rasolapN AlqawaAy^imi , meaning A she-camel loose, or slack, [ in the legs, and] soft in the joints [ thereof ]. (TA. [See also another meaning assigned to this phrase in what follows.]) ― -b4- Applied to hair, i. q. ↓ musotarosilN ; (S, K; in the CK murosal ;) which means Lank; not crisp: (Mgh, Msb: [and so accord. to an explanation of Astrsl in the S and K:]) or lank and pendent: (Msb:) or long, and lank or pendent. (AZ, Az, Msb.) ― -b5- And rasolapN , (M,) or rasolapu AlqawAy^imi , [of which see an explanation in what precedes,] (L, TA,) and ↓ mirosaAlN , applied to a she-camel, (M, L, TA,) Having much hair, (M,) or much and long hair, (L, TA,) upon her shanks, or hind legs ( fiY saAqiyohaA ): (M, L, TA:) but in the K, rasolapN and ↓ muraAsilN [not mirosaAlN ] are explained as epithets applied to a woman, meaning having much and long hair upon her shanks. (TA.) ― -b6- Also sing. of ↓ risaAlN , (TA,) which signifies The legs of a camel: (AZ, S, K, TA:) so called because of their length. (AZ, TA.) -A2- See also muraAsilN . -A3- And see the paragraph here next following.

definition: Gentleness; and a deliberate, or leisurely, manner of acting or behaving; as also ↓ risolapN ; (M, K;) [and perhaps ↓ rasolN and ↓ rasolapN ; for] one says AifoEalo ka*aA waka*aA EalaY risolika (S,...
sourceDefinition: Gentleness; and a deliberate, or leisurely, manner of acting or behaving; as also ↓ risolapN ; (M, K;) [and perhaps ↓ rasolN and ↓ rasolapN ; for] one says AifoEalo ka*aA waka*aA EalaY risolika (S, Mgh, * Msb, * CK * [but not in my MS. copy of the K nor in the copies used by SM]) and rasolika and rasolatika , (CK, [but likewise wanting in MS. copies of the K,]) i. e. [ Do thou such and such things ] at thine ease; (Msb;) or act thou gently, deliberately, or leisurely, (S, Mgh, K, *) in doing such and such things; like as one says, EalaY hiynatika . (S.) Sakhr-el-Ghei says, when despairing of his companions' overtaking him, his enemies surrounding him, and he feeling sure of slaughter, (M,) lawo A^an~a HawoliY mino qurayomK rajolaA biyDa Alwajuwhi yaHomiluwna Aln~abolaA lamanaEuwniY najodapF A^awo risolaA (Skr, M, *) i. e. [ If there were around me, of the family of Kureym, men on foot, fair in the faces (app. meant tropically), bearing arrows, they would defend me ] by violent means or by gentle means: (Skr:) or with fighting or without fighting. (M.) [See also a phrase cited from a trad. in what follows of this paragraph.] One says also, ↓ jaAw^uwA risolapF risolapF They came company by company. (M.) ― -b2- And A soft, gentle, saying or speech. (TA.) -A2- Also Milk, (S, M, K,) of whatever sort it be: (M, K:) or, accord. to the Towsheeh, fresh milk. (TA.) One says, kavura Alr~isolu AlEaAma , meaning Milk has become abundant this year: and the people of the desert assert that, when this is the case, dates are few; and that, when dates are abundant, milk is scarce. (TA.) ― -b2- It is said in a trad. [respecting the giving of the poor-rate], A_il~aA mano A^aEoTaY fiY najodatihaA warisolihaA , (S, TA,) which is explained in two different ways: (TA:) [J says that] it is from risolN in the sense first explained above; meaning straitness and plenty; i. e. Except him who gives when they are fat and goodly, when it is difficult, or hard, to their owner to give them forth, and when they are lean, [or] in a middling condition: (S:) and A'Obeyd says the like; and that it is similar to the saying, qaAla fulaAnN ka*aA Eam~aA risolihi , meaning Such a one said such a thing holding it (the saying) in light estimation: others say that it is from risolN signifying “ milk; ” which A'Obeyd disallows: IAth says that what is meant by njdp is straitness and drought or barrenness or dearth; and by rsl , plenty, and abundance of herbage or the like; because rsl , i. e. milk, is plentiful only in the case of abundance of herbage; so that the meaning is, except him who gives forth the due of God in the case of straitness and in that of plenty. (TA.) -A3- The risolaAni of a horse are The extremities of the EaDudaAni [or two arms ]. (M, K. *)

definition: Camels: (M, K:) thus expl.
sourceDefinition: Camels: (M, K:) thus expl. by A'Obeyd, without any epithet: (M:) or a drove, or herd, or a distinct collection or number, of camels, (S, M, * Msb, K,) and of sheep or goats, (S, K,) accord. to ISk from ten to twenty-five, (TA,) or the rasal of the watering-trough is at least ten, and extending to twenty-five; and the word is masc. and fem.; (M;) and also (assumed tropical:) of horses or horsemen; (S;) applied to (tropical:) a company of men (Mgh, Msb) as being likened to a drove, or herd, of camels: (Msb:) and also a distinct collection or number of any things: (M, K:) pl. A^arosaAlN . (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K.) A rájiz says, yaA *aAy^idayohaA xaw~iSaA biA^arosaAlo walaA ta*uwdaAhaA *iyaAda AlD~ul~aAlo [ O ye two drivers of them, water some before others, by droves, and drive them not with the driving of those who err from the right way ]: (S, TA:) i. e. bring near your camels some after some, and do not let them crowd upon the water-ing-trough. (TA.) And one says, jaA='ati AlA_ibilu rasalFA The camels came [ in a drove, or] following one another. (IAmb, TA.) And jaA='ati Alxayolu A^arosaAlFA , i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ The horses, or horsemen, came ] in successive distinct companies. (S, TA.) And jaA'uwA A^arosaAlFA (tropical:) They (men) came in successive companies. (Msb. [And the like is said in the Mgh and in the TA.]) waqiyrN kaviyru Alr~asali qaliylu Alr~isoli , occurring in a trad. relating to a drought, is said by IKt to mean [ A collection of sheep or goats ] of which many were sent to the pasture, i. e. many in number, but having little milk but the more probable explanation of kvyr Alrsl is that of El-'Odhree, who says that it means much dispersed in search of pasture: for the trad. relates that the camels had died, notwithstanding their ability to endure drought: how then should the sheep or goats be safe, and increase so as to become numerous? (IAth, TA.) ― -b2- Also Animals, or beasts, having milk. (M, TA.)

sourceDefinition: i. q. risaAlapN : (S, M, K:) see the latter, in five places. ― -b2- Hence, as meaning *uw rasuwlK , i. e. *uw risaAlapK [ One who has a message; i. e. a messenger ]; (TA;) i. q. ↓ murosalN , (S, M, K,) meaning one sent with a message; (S;) of the measure faEuwlN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN [or rather mufoEalN ]: (Msb:) [and often meaning an apostle of God; and with the article Al especially applied to Mohammad:] accord. to IAmb, its meaning in the proper language of the Arabs is one who carries on by consecutive progressions the relation of the tidings of him who has sent him; taken from the phrase jaA='ati AlA_ibilu rasalFA , meaning “ The camels came following one another: ” and the saying of the Muëdhdhin, A^a$ohadu A^an~a muHam~adFA rasuwlu A@ll~`h means I know [or acknowledge ] and declare that Mohammad is the relater by consecutive progressions of the tidings from God: (TA:) [or, as commonly understood, I testify that Mohammad is the apostle of God: ] a rasuwl is also called ↓ mirosaAlN , as being likened to the arrow thus termed: (TA:) the pl. of rasuwlN is rusulN (S, M, Msb, K) and rusolN (S, Msb) and rusalaA='N , (M, K,) which last is from IAar, (M,) or Fr, (Sgh,) and A^arosulN , (M, K,) which [is a pl. of pauc., and] occurs in the saying of the Hudhalee, lawokaAna fiY qalobiY kaqadori qulaAmapK HubFA ligayoriki qado A^ataAhaA A^arosuliY [ Had there been in my heart as much as a nailparing of love for another than thee, my messengers (or, accord. to the TA, app., my messages ) had come to her ]: respecting which IJ says that he has given to rasuwlN this form of pl., which is [regularly] proper to feminines [of this class of words, consisting of four letter whereof the third is a letter of prolongation], such as A^ataAnN and EanaAqN and EuqaAbN , because women are meant thereby, as they, generally, are the persons required to serve in cases of this kind: (M:) [for] rasuwlN is applied without variation to a male and a female, and to one [and to two] and to a pl. number; (S, M, Msb, K;) sometimes: (M:) i. e., it is allowable thus to apply it: (Msb:) hence, (S, K,) in the Kur [xxvi. 15], (S,) A_in~aA rasuwlu rab~i AlEaAlamiyna [ Verily we are the apostles of the Lord of the beings of the whole world ]: (S, K:) MF says, in ch. xx. [verse 49], we find A_in~aA rasuwlaA rab~ika [ Verily we are the two apostles of thy Lord ]; the dual form being here used: and Z says, in the Ksh, that in this instance it means the messengers, and therefore the dual form is necessarily used; but in ch. xxvi. it means the message, and therefore it is allowable to use it alike, when applying it as an epithet, as sing. and dual and pl.: Aboo-Is-hak the Grammarian says that the meaning here is, A_in~aA risaAlapN rab~i AlEaAlamiyna , i. e. *awuw risAlapi [ Verily we are those that have the message &c.]: (TA:) [but] rasuwlN [as meaning a messenger ] is like Eaduw~N and SadyqN [&c.] in its being used alike as masc. and fem. and sing. [and dual] and pl.: (Sgh, TA:) Aboo-Dhu-eyb uses it in the sense of rusul in his saying, A^alikoniY A_ilayohaA waxayoru Alr~asuw li A^aEolamuhumo binawaAHiY Alxabaro [ Be thou my messenger to her: and the best of messengers is the most knowing of them in respect of the bounds, or limits, of the tidings ]. (M.) See 4. The saying in the Kur [xxv. 39], waqawoma nuwHK lam~a ka*~abuwA Alr~usula A^agoraqonaAhumo [lit. And the people of Noah, when they charged with lying the apostles, we drowned them ], Zj says, may mean that they charged with lying Noah alone; for he who charges with lying a prophet charges therewith all the prophets, since they believe in God and in all his apostles; or the general term may be here used as meaning one; like as when you say, A^anota mim~ano yunofiqu Ald~araAhima , meaning “ Thou art of those who expend the kind of things termed drAhm . ” (M.) ― -b3- One says also, Als~ihaAmu rusulu AlmanaAyaA (tropical:) [ Arrows are the messengers of death, or of the decrees of death ]. (TA.) ― -b4- See also the next paragraph.

definition: Easy: occurring in the saying of Jubeyhà El-Asadee, waqumotu rasiylFA biAl~a*iY jaA='a yabotagiY A_ilayohi baliyja Alwajohi lasotu bibaAsiri [ And I undertook, or managed, with ease, that which he came seeking to obtain;
sourceDefinition: Easy: occurring in the saying of Jubeyhà El-Asadee, waqumotu rasiylFA biAl~a*iY jaA='a yabotagiY A_ilayohi baliyja Alwajohi lasotu bibaAsiri [ And I undertook, or managed, with ease, that which he came seeking to obtain; bright in countenance to him: I was not frowning ]. (TA.) -A2- Also A stallion-camel (K, * TA) of the Arabian race, that is sent among the $awol [or she-camels that have passed seven or eight months since the period of their bringing forth ] in order that he may leap them: one says, h`*aA rasiylu baniY fulaAnK This is the stallion of the camels of the sons of such a one: and A^arosala banuw fulaAnK rasiylahumo [ The sons of such a one sent the stallion of their camels ]: as though it were of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure mufoEalN , from A^arosala . (TA.) ― -b2- And accord. to some, A horse that is started with another in a race. (Har p. 544.) ― -b3- [In the CK and in a MS. copy of the K, voce EamuwdN , it occurs as though meaning The scout, or emissary, or perhaps the advanced guard, of an army: but in other copies of the K, in this instance, accord. to the TA, and in the L, the word is ray^iys .] ― -b4- I. q. ↓ muraAsilN [as meaning one who interchanges messages or letters with another: see 3]. (S, K.) ― -b5- The person who stands with thee ( AlmuwaAqifu laka [in the K (in which this explanation is erroneously assigned to ↓ rasuwlN ) AlmuwaAfiqu laka in a competition in shooting and the like: (M:) [i. e.] rasiylu Alr~ajuli signifies he who stands with the man, ( yaqifu maEahu , Har p. 544,) or he who acts interchangeably, or alternates, with the man, ( yuraAsiluhu , S,) in a competition in shooting, or in some other performance. (S and Har.) And, as also ↓ muraAsilN , One who relieves, or aids, another, in singing and in work, [ by alternating with him, i. e.,] in the former case, by taking up the strain when the other is unable to continue it [ so as to accomplish the cadence (see 6)], and in the latter case by taking up the work when the other is unable to continue it; or one who so relieves, or aids, another in singing with a high voice; i. q. mutaAlK : or one who aids another, [or relieves him, by alternating with him, ] or who follows him, or imitates him, in his work. (IAar, Msb.) One says, huwa rasiyluhu fiY AlginaA='i wanaHowihi [ He is the person who relieves him, or aids him, by alternating with him, in singing and the like thereof ]. (TA.) ― -b6- See also risaAlapN , in two places. -A3- Also Wide, or ample. (K.) ― -b2- A thing little in quantity, or incomplete: Al$~aYo'u All~aTiyfu in the copies of the K should be Al$~aYo'u AlT~afiyfu , as in the Moheet (TA.) ― -b3- And Sweet water. (K.)

definition: (S, M, Msb, K) and ↓ rasaAlapN (M, K) and ↓ rasuwlN (S, M, Msb, K) and ↓ rasiylN (Th, M, K) signify the same, (S, M, Msb, K,) A message;
sourceDefinition: (S, M, Msb, K) and ↓ rasaAlapN (M, K) and ↓ rasuwlN (S, M, Msb, K) and ↓ rasiylN (Th, M, K) signify the same, (S, M, Msb, K,) A message; and a letter; (MA in explanation of the first, and KL in explanation of the first and third;) [ a communication sent from one person or party to another, oral or written; ] substs. from A^arosala A_ilayohi : (M, K: *) the pl. of the first is rasaAy^ilu ; (Msb;) and A^arosulN is pl. of ↓ rasuwlN in the sense of risaAlapN , and of the fem. gender. (TA. [See the former of the two verses cited voce rasuwlN .]) You say, A^arosalotu fulaAnFA fiY risaAlapK : (S:) and A^arosala A_ilayohi ↓ rasuwlFA : (MA:) see 4. A poet says, (S,) namely El-Ash'ar El-Joafee, (TA,) ↓ A^alaA A^abolgo A^abaA EamorKw rasuwlFA biA^an~iY Eano futaAHatikumo ganiY~u [ Now deliver thou to Aboo-' Amr a message, saying that I am in no need of your judging ]: (S:) or baniY EamorKw [ the sons of ' Amr ]: he means, Eano Hukomkumo . (TA.) And hence the saying of Kutheiyir, laqado ka*aba AlwaA$uwna maA buHotu Einodahumo ↓ bisir~K walaA A^arosalotuhumo birasuwli [ Assuredly the slanderers have lied: I revealed not in their presence a secret, nor did I send them with a message ]: (S, TA:) or, as some relate the second hemistich, (TA,) ↓ bilayolaY walaA A^arosalotuhumo birasiyli [i. e. I revealed not the case of Leyla, nor did I send them with a message ]: thus cited by Th. (M, TA.) ― -b2- risaAlapN also signifies [ A tract, or small treatise or discourse; ] a majal~ap [i. e. book, or writing, relating to science, or on any subject. ] comprising a few questions, inquiries, or problems, of one kind: pl. rasaAy^ilu . (TA.) ― -b3- And Apostleship; the apostolic office or function. (MA.) ― -b4- A^um~u risaAlapa [in a copy of the K A^um~u risaAlapK ] The raxamap [or female of the vultur percnopterus, in the CK raHomap ]: (M, K, TA:) a surname thereof. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (Th, S, &c.,) aor. , (Th, TA,) inf. n. rukuwEN (Th, S, Mgh, Msb, K) and rakoEN , (Th, TA,) He bowed, or bent, himself; or became bowed or bent: (Th, S, Mgh, Msb:) so says Er-Rághib, adding that it is sometimes used to denote a particular manner of doing so in prayer, and sometimes to denote humility and self-abasement either in worship or in other cases: (TA:) he lowered his head: (Th:) and he (an old man) bowed himself, or bent himself, or became bowed or bent, by reason of age: (S, Msb, K:) this is [said to be] the primary signification: (TA:) or he fell upon his face; (IDrd, IB, K;) and stumbled. (IB.) ― -b2- And hence, from rakaEa as used in the first of the senses explained above, (S, Mgh,) or as used in the first of the senses assigned to it above when said of an old man, (TA,) or as used in the last sense explained above, (IB,) rukuwEu AlS~alaApi , (S, IB, Mgh, TA,) or Alr~ukuwEu fiY AlS~alaAp , The lowering of the head, (K, TA,) by a person praying, (TA,) [or in prayer, ] after the act of standing in which the recitation [ of portions of the Kur-án ] is performed, so that the palms of the hands reach the knees; or, so that the back becomes depressed; (K, TA;) accord. to the doctors of practical law, so that if a cup full of water be placed upon the back, it will not be spilled. (TA.) ― -b3- rakaEa A_ilaY A@ll~`hi He lowered his head, or he humbled himself, to God; syn. AiTomaA^an~a . (Z, TA.) ― -b4- rakaEa , also signifies He prayed; (Mgh;) and so ↓ trk~E . (TA.) Thus in the Kur [ii. 40], waA@rokaEuwA maEa Alr~aAkiEiyna , And pray ye with those who pray. (Mgh.) You say also, rakaEa rakoEapF , and rakoEatayoni , and valaAva rakaEaAtK , He prayed a rek'ah, and two rek'ahs, and three rek'ahs. (K.) [See rakoEapN , below.] ― -b5- Also, accord. to IKoot and several others, He stood to prayer. (Msb) ― -b6- lagibati AlA_ibilu Hat~aY rakaEato (tropical:) The camels became fatigued, or fatigued in the utmost degree, or languid in consequence of fatigue, so that they lowered their heads, and fell upon their faces. (TA.) ― -b7- rakaEati Aln~axolapu (assumed tropical:) The palm-tree inclined: a phrase which may be of classical authority, but [Mtr says,] I have not found it. (Mgh.) ― -b8- Said of a man, (TA,) rakaEa , also signifies (tropical:) He became poor after richness, or competence, or sufficiency; and his state, or condition, became lowered, or abased. (K, TA.)

definition: , [inf. n. of un. of 1: and particularly signifying] A single act of standing in prayer: and in its legal acceptation, used in a more particular sense; (Msb;) meaning a single act of standing in...
sourceDefinition: , [inf. n. of un. of 1: and particularly signifying] A single act of standing in prayer: and in its legal acceptation, used in a more particular sense; (Msb;) meaning a single act of standing in prayer, followed by the rukuwE [or lowering of the head in the manner described above (see Alr~ukuwEu fiY AlS~alaApi in the first paragraph)] and two prostrations: (TA:) [and hence, by a further extension of the meaning, for SalaApu rakoEapK , the prayer of one bowing of the head and body; the previous act of standing, and the two subsequent prostrations, being understood as included in this expression:] pl. rakaEaAtN . (Msb, K.) [Using it in the last of these senses,] you say, Sal~aY rakoEapF [ He performed the prayer of one bowing of the head and body ]: (K:) and Sal~aY rakoEatayoni [ he performed the prayers of two bowings of the head and body ]. (Msb, K.) [A full description of the act of prayer thus termed may be seen in my work on the Modern Egyptians.]

sourceDefinition: ; and ↓ ranima , (S, Msb,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. [ ranamN and] raniymN ; (TK;) i. q. raj~aEa Sawotahu (S, Msb) i. e. [ He trilled, or quavered; or] he reiterated his voice in his throat, or fauces, (S and K and TA in art. rjE ,) like [ as is done in ] chanting, (S in that art.,) or in reading or reciting, or singing, or piping, or other performances, of such as are accompanied with quavering, or trilling: (TA in that art.:) both said of a singer: (Msb:) and the former said of a bird, in its hadiyr [or cooing]; (S, Msb;) and of a bow, when it is twanged: (S:) and taroniymN [inf. n. of ↓ rn~m ] signifies the like: (S:) or Alt~aroniymu signifies taToriybu AlS~awoti [i. e. the trilling, or quavering, and prolonging the voice; or prolonging the voice, and modulating it sweetly, or warbling ]; (T, * M, K;) and so raniymN [mentioned above as inf. n. of ↓ ranima ]; (Lth, T, M, K;) whence Alt~aran~umu [which signifies the same, as is shown by what follows]: (Lth, T:) ↓ rn~m is said of the pigeon, (M, K,) and of the [bird called] muk~aA' , (M,) and of the [locust, or species of locust, called] junodab [meaning it chirped ], and of the bow [meaning it emitted a musical ringing sound, or a plaintive sound (see taronamuwtN , below,) when twanged], (M, K,) and [in like manner] of the lute, (M,) and of a thing (M, K:) of any kind (M) of which the sound is esteemed pleasant, or delightful; and taran~ama likewise: (M, K:) or you say, AlHamaAmapu tataran~amu [ The pigeon trills, or quavers, or cooes ]: and of the muk~aA=' you say, ↓ fiY Sawotihi taroniymN [ In its voice, or cry, is a trilling, or quavering ]: and of the bow, and the lute, and a thing [of any kind] of which the sound is esteemed pleasant, or delightful, ↓ lahu taroniymN [ It has a musical ringing sound, or a plaintive sound ]. (Lth, T.) It is said in a trad., maA A^a*ina A@ll~`hu li$aYo'K A^a*anahu linabiY~K Hasani Alt~aran~umi biAlquroA=ni [ God has not listened to anything as He listens to a prophet having a good manner of trilling, or quavering, or prolonging and modulating sweetly his voice, in reciting the Kur-án ]: or, as some relate it, Hasani AlS~awoti yataran~amu biAlquroA=ni [ good in respect of the voice, trilling, &c., in reciting the Kur-án ]. (TA.)

definition: A certain slender plant, (T, K,) well known;
sourceDefinition: A certain slender plant, (T, K,) well known; (T;) said by As to be one of the plants growing in plain, or soft, ground: (A'Obeyd, T:) IAar is related to have said that the ranamap , with n , is a certain species of tree: Sh knew not this word, and supposed it to be a mistranscription for ratamap ; but the ratam are [comparatively] large trees, [or rather shrubs, of the broom-kind,] having trunks; whereas the rnmp is of the slender kind of plants [as is said above]. (T.) -A2- See also the next preceding paragraph, in two places.

sourceDefinition: , aor. yaruwdu , (T, S, A,) inf. n. rawadaAnN (A, TA) and rawodN , (K, TA,) He, or it, (a thing, S,) came and went; (T, S, A, K;) [ went to and fro; ] was restless, or unsettled. (T, TA.) One says, maA liY A^araAka taruwdu muno*u Alyawomi [ What aileth me that I see thee coming and going, or going to and fro, during this day? ]. (A, TA.) And raAdato , (S, M, A, K,) aor. taruwdu , (S, A,) inf. n. rawadaAnN (S, M, K) and rawodN and ruw^uwdN , (M,) She (a woman) went about to and from the tents, or houses, of her female neighbours. (S, M, A, K.) And rAdt AlA_ibilu , aor. taruwdu , (AHn, M,) inf. n. riyaAdN (AHn, S, M, K) [and app. rawadaAnN &c. as above], The camels went to and fro in the place of pasture. (AHn, S, M, K.) And rAd Aln~aEamu fiY AlmaroEiY , inf. n. ryaAdN , The cattle went to and fro in the place of pasture. (A.) And rAdt Ald~awaAb~u , inf. n. rawodN and rawadaAnN [and app. riyaAdN also]; and ↓ AstrAdt ; The beasts pastured [ going to and fro ]. (M.) And rAdt Alr~KyHu , (T, M,) aor. taruwdu , (TA,) inf. n. rawadaAnN (T, TA) and rawodN and ruw^uwd , (TA,) The wind became in motion, or in a state of commotion: (T, TA:) or veered about. (M, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] rAd wisaAduhu [lit. His pillow moved to and fro; meaning] (tropical:) he was, or became, restless, (S, A,) by reason of disease or anxiety: (A:) [or he was, or became, sleepless: for] a poet uses the phrase raA*a wisaAduhaA as expressive of an imprecation, mean ing (assumed tropical:) May she be sleepless, so that her pillow may not remain still. (TA.) [And rAd xurotu Alqawomi and rAdt A^axoraAtuhumo : see xurotN .] -A2- rAd , aor. yaruwdu , (Msb,) inf. n. riyaAdN (Msb, K) and rawodN ; (K;) and ↓ ArtAd , (Msb,) inf. n. AirotiyaAdN ; (K;) and ↓ AstrAd ; (TA;) He sought, sought after, or desired; or he sought, or desired, to find and take, or to get; (Msb, K;) a thing. (Msb.) [It seems to imply the going to and fro in seeking.] You say, rAd AlkalaA^a , (S, A, Mgh, L,) and AlmaA='a , (Mgh,) aor. yaruwdu , (S, A, Mgh, L,) inf. n. riyaAdN and rawodN : (S, L;) and ↓ ArtAdhu ; (S, A, Mgh, L;) [and ↓ Astrdhu , as appears from what follows;] and simply rAd ; (L;) He sought after herbage, (S, Mgh, L,) and water. (Mgh.) And rAd A^aholahu kalaA^F , and manozilFA , (M, L,) and rAd lahumo kalaA^F , and manozilFA , inf. n. rawodN (T, M, L) and riyaAdN ; (M;) and ↓ ArdtAd ; (T, M, L;) and ↓ AstrAd ; (M, L;) He looked for, (T,) and sought after, herbage, and a place in which to alight, (T, M, L,) and chose the best [ that he could find ], (T,) for his family. (T, M, L.) And AlT~ayoru ↓ tasotariydu The birds seek after their sustenance, going to and fro in search of it. (A.) [Hence,] libawolihi ↓ ArtAd He sought a soft place, (S, Mgh, L,) or a sloping place, (S, L,) for his urine. when he desired to void it, (S, Mgh, L,) lest it should return towards him, or sprinkle back upon him: (L:) from a trad. (S, L.) ― -b2- rAd Ald~aAra , aor. as above, He questioned, or interrogated, [respecting a person beloved,] the house, or abode. (M.) ― -b3- rudotu Ald~awaAb~a I pastured the beasts; as also ↓ A^aradotuhaA . (M.)

(T, TA.) One says, maA liY A^araAka taruwdu muno*u Alyawomi [ What aileth me that I see thee coming and going, or going to and fro, during this day? ]. (A, TA.) And raAdato , (S, M, A, K,) aor. taruwdu , (S, A,) inf. n. rawadaAnN (S, M, K) and rawodN and ruw^uwdN , (M,) She (a woman) went about to and from the tents, or houses, of her female neighbours. (S, M, A, K.) And rAdt AlA_ibilu , aor. taruwdu , (AHn, M,) inf. n. riyaAdN (AHn, S, M, K) [and app. rawadaAnN &c. as above], The camels went to and fro in the place of pasture. (AHn, S, M, K.) And rAd Aln~aEamu fiY AlmaroEiY , inf. n. ryaAdN , The cattle went to and fro in the place of pasture. (A.) And rAdt Ald~awaAb~u , inf. n. rawodN and rawadaAnN [and app. riyaAdN also]; and ↓ AstrAdt ; The beasts pastured [ going to and fro ]. (M.) And rAdt Alr~KyHu , (T, M,) aor. taruwdu , (TA,) inf. n. rawadaAnN (T, TA) and rawodN and ruw^uwd , (TA,) The wind became in motion, or in a state of commotion: (T, TA:) or veered about. (M, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] rAd wisaAduhu [lit. His pillow moved to and fro; meaning] (tropical:) he was, or became, restless, (S, A,) by reason of disease or anxiety: (A:) [or he was, or became, sleepless: for] a poet uses the phrase raA*a wisaAduhaA as expressive of an imprecation, mean ing (assumed tropical:) May she be sleepless, so that her pillow may not remain still. (TA.) [And rAd xurotu Alqawomi and rAdt A^axoraAtuhumo : see xurotN .] -A2- rAd , aor. yaruwdu , (Msb,) inf. n. riyaAdN (Msb, K) and rawodN ; (K;) and ↓ ArtAd , (Msb,) inf. n. AirotiyaAdN ; (K;) and ↓ AstrAd ; (TA;) He sought, sought after, or desired; or he sought, or desired, to find and take, or to get; (Msb, K;) a thing. (Msb.) (Mgh.) And rAd A^aholahu kalaA^F , and manozilFA , (M, L,) and rAd lahumo kalaA^F , and manozilFA , inf. n. rawodN (T, M, L) and riyaAdN ; (M;) and ↓ ArdtAd ; (T, M, L;) and ↓ AstrAd ; (M, L;) He looked for, (T,) and sought after, herbage, and a place in which to alight, (T, M, L,) and chose the best [ that he could find ], (T,) for his family. (T, M, L.) And AlT~ayoru ↓ tasotariydu The birds seek after their sustenance, going to and fro in search of it. (A.) [Hence,] libawolihi ↓ ArtAd He sought a soft place, (S, Mgh, L,) or a sloping place, (S, L,) for his urine. when he desired to void it, (S, Mgh, L,) lest it should return towards him, or sprinkle back upon him: (L:) from a trad. (S, L.) ― -b2- rAd Ald~aAra , aor. as above, He questioned, or interrogated, [respecting a person beloved,] the house, or abode. (M.) ― -b3- rudotu Ald~awaAb~a I pastured the beasts; as also ↓ A^aradotuhaA . (M.)

definition: He endeavoured to turn him [to, or from, a thing];
sourceDefinition: He endeavoured to turn him [to, or from, a thing]; as in the phrase rAwdhu EalaY AlA_isolaAmi He endeavoured to turn him, or convert him, to El-Islám; occurring in a trad., in which the agent of the verb is Mohammad, and the object is his uncle Aboo-Tálib;. syn. raAjaEahu and raAd~ahu : (L:) or raAwadotuhu EalaY ka*aA , (S,) or EalaY AlA^amori , (Msb,) inf. n. muraAwadapN and riwaAdN , (S, Msb, K,) [primarily] signifies I desired, (S, Msb, K, *) or sought, (Msb,) of him that he should do such a thing, or the thing; (S, * Msb;) AlmuraAwadapu implying contention ( AlmuxaASamap ), because he who desires, or seeks, affects gentle, or bland, behaviour, like him who deceives, or beguiles, and, like him, strives, or labours, to attain his object: (Msb:) and [hence,] rAwdhu Eani AlA^amori , and Ealayohi , He endeavoured to turn him by blandishment, or by deceitful arts, or to entice him to turn, from the thing, and to it; syn. daAraAhu , (M, L,) or raAdaAhu . (TT, as from the M.) sanuraAwidu Eanohu A^abaAhu , in the Kur xii. 61, means [ We will endeavour to turn his father from him, by blandishment, or artifice, and to make him yield him to us: or] we will strive, or labour, to obtain him of his father. (Bd, Jel.) And raAwadatohu Eano nafosihi [in the Kur xii. 23] (assumed tropical:) She desired, or sought, of him, copulation, or his lying with her, using blandishment, or artifice, for that purpose; she tempted him to lie with her: (T, and Bd in xii. 23:) [more literally, she endeavoured to turn him, or entice him, by blandishment, or deceitful arts, from his disdain, or disdainful incompliance, and to make him yield himself to her: ] and raAwadahaA Eano nafosihaA (assumed tropical:) he desired, or sought, of her, copulation, &c. (T.) And raAwadahu Eano nafosihi (tropical:) He endeavoured to deceive him, or beguile him, and to turn him [ from his disdain, or purpose, or will, ] by blandishment, or artifice. (A.)

definition: , (S, A, K,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, K,) inf. n. A_irowaAdN and murowadN and [quasi-inf. n.] ↓ marowadN (S, K) and ↓ ruwayodN (TA as from the K [but omitted in my MS. copy of the K and in the CK]) and ↓ ruwayodaA='u and ↓ ruwayodiyapN or ↓ ruwayodiy~apN , (accord. to different copies of the K,) He acted, or proceeded, gently, softly, or in a leisurely manner, (S, A, K, TA,) in going, or pace. (S, A, TA.) -A2- A^arowadahu , (S,) inf. n. A_irowaAdN , (M,) He acted gently, softly, or in a leisurely manner, towards, or with, him; or granted him a delay, or respite; let him alone, or left him, for a while; syn. A^amohalahu . (S, M. *) ― -b2- A^aradotu Ald~awaAb~a : see 1, last sentence. -A3- A^araAdahu , (M, L, Msb,) inf. n. A_iraAdapN , (S, M, L, Msb, K,) originally with w , [i. e. A^arowadahu ,] because you say raAwadahu (S, L) in a similar sense, (L,) He willed, wished, or desired, it: (S, * M, L, K: *) he loved, or liked, it; and cared for, or minded, it; or was rendered thoughtful, careful, or anxious, by it: (M, L:) or he desired it; sought it, or sought after it; ( Talabahu ;) and chose it: (Msb:) [or] it differs from Talabahu , inasmuch as A_iraAdapN is sometimes merely conceived in the mind, not apparent; whereas TalabN is never other wise than apparent, either by act or by word: (Aboo-'Obeyd El-Bekree, TA:) Th says that it sometimes denotes loving, or liking, and some times it does not [as will be shown by what follows]: and Lh mentions the saying harodtu Al$~aYo'a , aor. A^uhariyduhu , inf. n. hiraAdapN , with h substi tuted for ' [as in haraqotu for A^araqotu , &c.]. (M.) You say, A^aradotu minohu ka*aA [ I desired, of him, such a thing ]. (A.) And maA A^aradotu A_il~aA maA faEalota [ I desired not aught save what thou didst, or hast done ]. (A.) [And ArAd bihi ka*aA He desired to do to him, or he intended him, such a thing; whether good or evil: see Kur xxxiii. 17, &c.] And Kutheiyir says, A^uriydu liA^anosaY *ikorahaA fakaA^an~amaA tumav~alu liY layolaY bikul~i sabiyli [ I desire to forget the remembrance of her, or the mention of her; but it seems as though Leylà were imaged to me in every road ]; meaning A^uriydu A^ano A^anosaY . (M.) [And ISd says,] I think that Sb has mentioned the phrase A^araAdaniY bih`*aAlika , i. e. He intended, or meant, me by that. (M.) [ ArAd often signifies He intended, or meant, such a thing by a saying or an action.] fawajadaA fiyhaA jidaArFA yuriydu A^ano yanoqaD~a , in the Kur xviii. 78, means (tropical:) [ And they found therein a wall ] that was near, or about, to fall down, (Bd, Jel,) or that was ready to fall down; though AlA_iraAdap is only from an animate being, and not properly predicable of a wall: and there are many similar instances; as the saying of a poet, yuriydu Alr~umoHu Sadora A^abiY baraA='K wa yaEodilu Eano rimaA='i baniY Euqayoli [ The spear is ready to pierce the breast of Aboo Barà, but it turns away from the bloods of the sons of 'Okeyl ]. (M.) [In like manner also] one says, ArAd AlbukaA='a (assumed tropical:) [ He was about, or ready, to weep: a phrase of frequent occurrence; like tahay~aA^a lilobukaA='i , and ham~a biAlobukaA='i ]. (TA in art. jh$ , &c.) ― -b2- You say also, ArAdhu EalaY Al$~aYo'i , (M,) or ElY AlA^amori , (A, Mgh,) He endeavoured to induce him, (M,) or he incited him, or made him, (A, Mgh,) to do the thing. (M, A, Mgh.) And ArAdhu EalaY A^ano yakotuba He incited him, or made him, to write. (Mgh.) And ArAdhu A_ilaY AlkalaAmi He constrained, or necessitated, him to speak. (M, * TA.)

sourceDefinition: Gentleness; or a leisurely manner of acting or proceeding. (S, M, A, K.) [And accord. to the TT, as from the M, so ruw^odN ; but this is a mistranscription, for ruw^odN : see this last, in art. rA^d .] You say, yamo$iY EalaY ruwdK He walks, or goes, gently, softly, or in a leisurely manner. (T.)

sourceDefinition: [act. part. n. of 1, Coming and going; moving to and fro; &c.]. [Hence,] AimoraA^apN raAy^idapN : see raAdN . And dawaAb~u rawaAy^idu [pl. of daAb~apN raAy^idapN ] Beasts pasturing at pleasure: (T:) or going to and for [ in the place of pasture ]: or pasturing together while the rest are debarred from the pasture, or tied. (M.) And riyHN raAy^idapN : see raAdN , last two sentences. And raAy^idu AlwisaAdi [lit. Whose pillow moves to and fro; meaning] (tropical:) a man restless by reason of disease or anxiety; (A;) or uneasy on his pillow by reason of anxiety that disquiets him: (TA:) [or sleepless: see 1.] And raAy^idu AlEayoni The Euw~aAr of the eye, [i. e. the mote, or the like, that has fallen into it, or the foul, thick, white matter that collects in its inner corner, and ] that moves to and fro ( yaruwdu ) therein. (S.) ― -b2- The handle of the hand-mill, (S, M, A, K,) which the grinder grasps (S, M, A) when he turns round the mill-stone (S, A) therewith. (A.) ― -b3- See also mirowadN . ― -b4- One who is sent (S, M, A, Mgh, L, K) before a people or party (Mgh) to seek for herbage (S, M, A, Mgh, L, K) and water (Mgh) and the places where rain has fallen; (L;) or one who looks for, and seeks, herbage, and a place in which to alight, and chooses the best thereof; (T;) and ↓ raAdN signifies the same; (S, M, K;) the latter occurring in the poetry of Hudheyl; (M;) [originally rawadN ,] of the measure faEalN in the sense of the measure faAEilN , (S, K,) like faraTN in the sense of faAriTN , (S,) or of the measure faAEilN deprived of its medial radical letter, or of the measure faEilN , [originally rawidN ,] but if so, it is a kind of rel. n., not an act. part. n.: (M:) the pl. of the former is ruw~aAdN (M, A, L) and raAdapN . (L.) One says, Alr~aAy^idu laA yako*ibu A^aholahu , (T, Mgh,) or laA yako*ibu Alr~aAy^idu A^aholahu , (S,) [ The seeker of herbage, &c., will not lie to his family, ] for if he lie to them he perishes with them: (Ham p. 547:) a prov. applied to him who will not lie when he relates a thing. (M.) And hence the saying, AlHum~aY raAy^idu Almawoti (tropical:) Fever is the messenger that precedes death; like the messenger that goes before a people, or party, to seek for herbage and water. (Mgh, TA.) Hence, likewise, raAy^idN is also applied to (tropical:) One who goes before with some abominable deed or design. (TA.) And to (assumed tropical:) A seeker of science or knowledge. (L, from a trad.) [Hence also,] A^anaA raAy^idu HaAjapK and ↓ murotaAduhaA (tropical:) [ I am the seeker of an object of want ]: and A^unaAsN ruw~aAdu AlHaAjaAti (tropical:) [ Men who are the seekers of the objects of want ]. (A.) ― -b5- Also One who has no place in which to alight or abide. (T in art. ryd and TA.) -A2- [See also art. rA^d .]

sourceDefinition: A certain well-known instrument, (Msb,) [ resembling a bodkin, or small probe, tapering towards the end, but blunt, generally of wood or bone or ivory or silver, ] with which the [ black powder called ] kuHol is applied to the eyes; (TA;) syn. miylN , (S, M, A, K,) and mikoHaAlN : so called [because it is passed to and fro along the edges of the eyelids,] from raAda signifying “he, or it, came and went:” (Mgh:) pl. maraAwidu . (M, K.) ― -b4- An iron [ swivel ] that turns round in the lijaAm [i. e. bit, or bit and bridle ]: (S, K:) or an iron [ swivel ] which is attached to the rasan of the colt [or horse ] and of the hawk, [i. e., to the halter, or leading-cord, of the colt or horse, and the leash of the hawk, ] and which, when he turns round, turns round with him: (A:) or the mirowadaAni , also called the ↓ raAy^idaAni , are the two rings in [ either of ] which is the extremity of the Ei*aAr [or side-piece of the headstall of the horse ]. (TA.)

definition: signifies The adorning, ornamenting, decorating, or embellishing, of a thing, (KL, and Har p.
sourceDefinition: signifies The adorning, ornamenting, decorating, or embellishing, of a thing, (KL, and Har p. 3,) primarily, with zuxoruf , i. e. gold: (Har ib.:) and hence, (Har,) the adorning, &c., of falsehood, or a lie: (KL, Har:) and the falsifying or adulterating [of speech &c.]. (KL.) You say, zaxorafa Albayota , inf. n. zaxorafapN , He adorned, ornamented, decorated, or embellished, the house, or chamber, &c.; and rendered it complete: and zuxorifa is said of anything as meaning It was adorned, ornamented, decorated, or embellished. (TA.) And zaxorafa AlkalaAma He arranged, or rightly disposed, or put into a right or proper state, the speech, or language: (TA:) and i. q. raq~a$ahu [i. e. he embellished it; generally meaning, with lies ]. (S, A, K, in art. rq$ .) [This verb is mentioned and explained by Freytag as on the authority of the K, in which it is not found in this art.]

definition: Gold: (Fr, S, M, K:) so in the Kur xvii.
sourceDefinition: Gold: (Fr, S, M, K:) so in the Kur xvii. 95: and this, accord. to ISd, is the primary meaning. (TA.) ― -b2- Then applied to Any orna- ment, decoration, or embellishment: (ISd, TA:) anything adorned, ornamented, decorated, or embellished: (Ham p. 784:) and particularly applied to the decorations, and pictured works, in gold, with which the Kaabeh was ornamented in Pagan times. (TA.) The colours of the plants or herbage, of land, (K, TA,) red and yellow and white: its ornature, consisting in blossoms and flowers: or its perfection: so in the Kur x. 25. (TA.) And The furniture, or utensils, of a house or tent. (TA.) ― -b3- Anything varnished, or embellished with a false colouring, or falsified, is likened thereto [and so termed]. (S, TA.) [Hence,] zuxorufu Alqawoli The ornature of speech; (TA;) the fair appearance, or comeliness, of speech, produced by the embellishing with lies: (K, TA:) so in the Kur vi. 112: (TA:) or it there means varnished falsehoods. (Bd.) ― -b4- [Its pl.] zaxaArifu signifies The lines, or streaks, [ that are seen on the surface ] of water. (S, K.) ― -b5- And Ships: (T, K:) or ornamented, or decorated, ships: (M, TA:) or the ornature of ships, with which they are decorated. ('Eyn, TA.) ― -b6- Also Certain insects that fly upon the water, (T, O, K,) having four legs, resembling the common fly; (O, K;) small flies, having four legs, that fly upon the water: (M, TA:) the sing., zuxorufN , is expl. by Kr [in the Munjid] as meaning a kind of flying thing. (TA.)

definition: The kind of verse, or poetry, [ more commonly ] termed rajaz : [hence,] a poet says, laA yugolabu Aln~aAziEu maA daAma Alz~amalo [ The drawer of water will not be overcome as long as the zml continues ];
sourceDefinition: The kind of verse, or poetry, [ more commonly ] termed rajaz : [hence,] a poet says, laA yugolabu Aln~aAziEu maA daAma Alz~amalo [ The drawer of water will not be overcome as long as the zml continues ]; meaning, as long as he recites [or chants] the verse termed rajaz [or zamal ], he is strong enough to work: thus it is related on the authority of AA: another reading is Alr~amalo : both are correct as to meaning. (IJ, TA.)

definition: A certain thing in which water is cooled: of the dial.
sourceDefinition: A certain thing in which water is cooled: of the dial. of El-'Irák: (K:) applied by the people of Baghdád to a green [ jar such as is called ] jar~ap or xaAbiyap , in the middle whereof is a perforation, in which is fixed a tube of silver or lead, whence one drinks; so called because it is wrapped ( tuzam~alu i. e. tulaf~u ) with a piece of cloth of coarse flax, or some other thing, between which and the jar is straw: it is in their houses in the days of summer: the water is cooled in the night by means of the [ porous earthen bottles called ] bar~aAdaAt ; then it is poured into this mzm~lp , and remains in it cool. (Har p. 548.)

definition: , (S, O, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: , (S, O, Msb, K, &c.,) aor. (O, Msb, K) and , (O, K,) but the former is of higher authority, or more usual, (O, TA,) inf. n. saboqN , (S, Msb,) He preceded him; he was, or became, got, went, or came, before him, or ahead of him; he outwent, or outstripped, him; he had, got, or took, precedence of him; syn. taqad~amahu ; (K, TA;) in running, and in everything. (TA.) Some read, in the Kur [xxi. 27], laA yasobuquwnahu biAlqawoli , thus, with damm, meaning They say not [anything] without his having taught them: (O, TA:) or they say not anything until He has said it: originally, laA yasobuiqu qawoluhumo qawolahu [ their saying does not precede his saying ]: this reading is from the phrase saAbaqotuhu fasabaqotuhu , [expl. below,] aor. of the latter A^asobuquhu . (Bd.) See 3. ― -b2- sabaqa Alfarasu fiY AlHalobapi The horse outstripped, or came in first, among those started together for a wager, or in the race-ground. (O, K.) Hence the trad. of 'Alee, sabaqa rasuwlu A@ll~`hi waSal~aY A^abuw bakorK waval~ava Eumaru (assumed tropical:) [ The Apostle of God came in first in the race, and Aboo-Bekr came in next, and 'Omar came in third ]. (O, TA.) [And sabaqa used in like manner with the objective complement understood means He preceded, &c., as above; and hence, he was, or became, first, foremost, or beforehand; he had, or got, the priority, or precedence. And He was, or became, one of the first or foremost: see saAbiqN . See also qaSabu Als~aboqi in art. qSb .] ― -b3- sabaqa Aln~aAsa A_ilaY AlA^amori [ He preceded the other people; was, or became, before them; or had, got, or took, precedence of them; in betaking, or applying, himself to the affair ]. sourceDefinition: , (inf. n. tasobiyqN , Mgh,) He took, or received, the sabaq [i. e. stake, or wager, laid at a race or a shooting-match, to be taken by the successful competitor ]: (IAar, O, K:) or sab~aqotuhu I took, or received, the sabaq , from him. (Az, Mgh, Msb.) ― -b2- And He gave the sabaq : (IAar, O, K:) or sab~aqotuhu I gave him the sabaq . (Az, Mgh, Msb.) Thus it has two contr. significations. (IAar, Az, Mgh, O, Msb, K.) Hence, in the trad. of Rukáneh the wrestler, maA tusab~iquniY , i. e. What wilt thou give me [if I overcome] ? and he said, The third of my sheep, or goats. (Mgh.) And sab~aqa Albadorapa bayona Al$~uEaraA='i (tropical:) He made the [ sum of money termed ] bdrp to be a sabaq [i. e. stake, or wager, ] among the poets, to be taken by him who should overcome. (Z, TA.) And it is said in a trad., A^amara biA_ijoraA='i Alxayoli wasb~aqahaA valaAvapa A^aEo*uqK mino valaAvi naxalaAtK , meaning [ He ordered the making of the horse to run, and ] gave them as a sabaq [ three racemes of dates from three palm-trees ]: or it may mean, he took, or received, as their sabaq : or it [i. e. sbqhA ] may be without teshdeed, [as a subst. with its affixed pronoun,] meaning the property assigned [ as their sabaq ]. (L, TA.) ― -b3- One says also, sab~aqotu bayona Alxayoli [app. meaning I gave a sabaq among the horses ]: (O:) or sab~aqotu Alxayola , and bayonahaA ↓ sAbqt , meaning I sent forth the horses with their riders upon them, to see which of them would outstrip. (TA.) ― -b4- And sb~qt Al$~aApu , inf. n. as above, The ewe, or she-goat, cast her young one, or fœtus, in an incomplete state: (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K:) but sb~gt , with g , is better known. (Ibn-'Abbád, O.) -A2- sab~aqotu AlT~aAy^ira (tropical:) I put the sibaAqaAni [or pair of jesses ] upon the legs of the bird, and [ so ] shackled it. (TA.)

definition: A stake, or wager, that is laid between the persons concerned in a race, (T, S, O, Mgh, * Msb, * K,) and in a shooting-match;
sourceDefinition: A stake, or wager, that is laid between the persons concerned in a race, (T, S, O, Mgh, * Msb, * K,) and in a shooting-match; in the former case taken by [ the owner of ] the one that outstrips; (T, TA:) and ↓ suboqapN signifies the same: (K:) pl. of the former A^asobaAqN . (O, K.) It is said in a trad., laA sabaqa A_il~aA fiY xuf~K A^awo HaAfirK A^awo naSolK , meaning There shall be no stake, or wager, except in the case of the racing of camels, or of horses or mules or asses, or in the case of [ the arrowhead or lance-head, i. e.] shooting or casting [the lance]: for all these affairs are preparations for engaging in fight with the enemy; and mules and asses are included because they carry the baggage of the army. (O, TA.) ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) The lesson of a boy, that is learned each day in the school; also called A_imaAmN . (TA in art. Am .)

definition: [act. part. n. of 1, Preceding, &c.: and sometimes it means one of the first or foremost: as is shown by what here follows]: sometimes what is thus termed has one coming up with it; as [sometimes...
sourceDefinition: [act. part. n. of 1, Preceding, &c.: and sometimes it means one of the first or foremost: as is shown by what here follows]: sometimes what is thus termed has one coming up with it; as [sometimes happens] in the case of the sAbq of horses: and sometimes it is like him who obtains the winning-cane ( qaSabap Als~aboq [see art. qSb ]); for he outstrips to it and has none to share with him in it, there being none coming up with him. (Msb.) It is applied to a horse That outstrips; as also ↓ sabuwqN : (T, Msb, TA: *) and the pl. [masc., i. e. pl. of the former,] applied to horses is sub~aqN and [fem., i. e. pl. of saAbiqapN ,] sawaAbiqu : (TA:) [or] sawaAbiqu may be pl. of saAbiqN regarded as a subst. like kaAhilN and gaAribN of which the pls. are kawaAhilu and gawaAribu . (Ham p. 46.) ― -b2- By the saAbiqaAt mentioned in the Kur lxxix. 4 are meant The angels that precede the devils with the revelation [ that they convey ] to the prophets: (TA:) or the angels that precede the jinn, or genii, in listening to the revelation: (T, K, TA:) or the angels that precede with the souls of the believers to Paradise (Bd, Jel) and with the souls of the unbelievers to Hell: (Bd:) or the horses [ that precede in battle ]: (Zj, TA:) or the souls of the believers, that go forth with ease: or the stars [ that precede other stars ]. (TA. [See more in the Expositions of Bd and others.]) ― -b3- [The pl.] sub~aqN , applied to palm-trees, means (assumed tropical:) That produce their fruit early. (TA.)

definition: He, or it, hit, or hurt, his saHor [or lungs, &c.
sourceDefinition: He, or it, hit, or hurt, his saHor [or lungs, &c.], (Mgh, TA,) or his suHorap [i. e. heart ]. (TA.) ― -b2- And the same, aor. , inf. n. siHorN , (T, TA,) [said to be] the only instance of a pret. and aor. and inf. n. of these measures except the verb faEala , aor. yafoEalu , inf. n. fiEolN , (MF,) (tropical:) He turned it, (T,) or him, (TA,) Eano wajohihi [ from its, or his, course, or way, or manner of being ]: and hence other significations here following. (T, TA. [Accord. to the T, this seems to be proper; but accord. to the A, tropical.]) In this sense the verb is used in the Kur xxiii. 91. (Fr.) The Arabs say to a man, maA saHaraka Eano wajohi ka*aA wa ka*aA (tropical:) What has turned thee from such and such a course? (Yoo.) A^ufika and suHira are syn. [as meaning (tropical:) He was turned from his course &c.]. (TA.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) He turned him from hatred to love. (TA.) ― -b4- Hence, (TA,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (T, S, TA,) and inf. n. also saHorN , (KL, TA,) (tropical:) He enchanted, or fascinated, him, or it; (S, * K, * KL, PS;) and so ↓ sH~rhu (MA, TA) [in an intensive or a frequentative sense, meaning he enchanted, or fascinated, him, or it, much, or (as shown by an explanation of its pass. part. n.) time after time ]: and saHara Eayonahu He enchanted, or fascinated, his eye. (MA.) You say, saHara Al$~aYo'a Eano wajohihi , meaning (tropical:) He (an enchanter, saAHirN ) apparently turned the thing from its proper manner of being, making what was false to appear in the form of the true, or real; causing the thing to be imagined different from what it really was. (T, TA. [See siHorN , below.]) And AlmaroA^apu tasoHaru Aln~aAsa biEayonihaA (tropical:) [ The woman enchants, or fascinates, men by her eye ]. (A.) And saHarahu bikalaAmihi (assumed tropical:) He caused him, or enticed him, to incline to him by his soft, or elegant, speech, and by the beauty of its composition. (Msb.) ― -b5- (tropical:) He deceived, deluded, beguiled, circumvented, or outwitted, him; (S, Mgh, K; *) as also ↓ sH~rhu , [but app. in an intensive or a frequentative sense,] (K, TA,) inf. n. tasoHiyrN . (TA. [Accord. to the Mgh, the former verb in this sense seems to be derived from the same verb in the first of the senses expl. in this art.]) ― -b6- And in like manner, (assumed tropical:) He diverted him [with a thing], as one diverts a child with food, that he may be contented, and not want milk; syn. Eal~alahu ; as also ↓ sH~rhu , inf. n. tasoHiyrN . (S, TA.) One says, saHarahu biAlT~aEaAmi wa Al$~araAbi , and ↓ sH~rhu , (assumed tropical:) He fed him, and diverted him [ from the feeling of want ], with meat and drink. (TA.) ― -b7- And saHarotu AlfiD~apa (assumed tropical:) I gilded the silver. (Ham p. 601.) ― -b8- siHorN is also syn. with fasaAdN [as quasi-inf. n. of A^afosada , as is indicated in the TA; thus signifying The act of corrupting, marring, spoiling, &c.: see the pass. part. n. masoHuwrN ]. (TA.) [Hence,] one says, saHara AlmaTaru AlT~iyna and Alt~uraAba , (assumed tropical:) The rain spoiled the clay, and the earth, or dust, so that it was not fit for use. (TA.) ― -b9- And one says of the adhesion of the lungs to the side by reason of thirst, yasoHaru A^alobaAna Alganami , meaning (assumed tropical:) It causes the milk of the sheep, or goats, to descend before bringing forth. (TA.) -A2- saHara also signifies He went, or removed, to a distance, or far away; syn. tabaAEada ; (T, K;) said of a man. (T, TA.) -A3- saHira , aor. , (assumed tropical:) He went forth early in the morning, in the first part of the day; or between the time of the prayer of daybreak and sunrise; syn. bak~ara . (O, K. [See also 4.])

sourceDefinition: , and ↓ saHarN , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) sometimes thus because of the faucial letter, (S,) and ↓ suHorN , (S, Msb, K,) and, accord. to El-Khafájee, in the 'Ináyeh, ↓ siHorN , but this is not mentioned by any other, and therefore requires confirmation, (TA,) The lungs, or lights: (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) or what adheres to the gullet and the windpipe, of [ the contents of ] the upper part of the belly: or all that hangs to the gullet, consisting of the heart and liver and lungs: (Msb, TA:) and the part of the exterior of the body corresponding to the place of the lungs: (Mgh, TA: *) and saHorN signifies also the liver; and the core, or black or inner part, ( sawaAd ,) and sides, or regions, of the heart: (TA:) and ↓ suHorN , the heart; (ElJarmee, K;) as also ↓ suHorapN : (TA:) the pl. (of saHorN , S, Msb) is suHuwrN , and (of ↓ suHorN , S, Msb, and of ↓ saHarN , Msb) A^asoHaArN . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- Hence, Ainotafaxa saHoruhu , (S, A, K,) and Ainotafaxato ↓ masaAHiruhu , (A, K,) (tropical:) His lungs became inflated, or swollen, by reason of timidity and cowardice: (A:) said of a coward: (S:) and of one who has exceeded his due bounds: Lth says that, when repletion arises in a man, one says Antfx sHrh , and that the meaning is, [as given also in the K,] he exceeded his due bounds: but Az says that this is a mistake, and that this phrase is only said of a coward, whose inside is filled with fear, and whose lungs are inflated, or swollen, so that the heart is raised to the gullet: and of the same kind is the phrase in the Kur [xxxiii. 10] wabalagati Alquluwbu AlHanaAjira . (TA.) ― -b3- And AlmuqaT~aEapu AlA^asoHaAri , and Als~uHuwri , (assumed tropical:) [ She that has her lungs burst asunder ], an appellation given to the A^aronab [i. e. hare, or female hare ], (S, K,) or to the swift Arnb , (TA in art. qTE ,) by way of good omen, meaning that her lungs will burst asunder; like AlmuqaT~aEapu Aln~iyaATi : (S:) and some (of those of later times, S) say AlmuqaT~iEapu , with kesr to the T ; (S, K;) as though, by her speed and vehemence of running, she would burst asunder her lungs; (S;) or because she bursts the lungs of the dogs by the vehemence of her running, and the lungs of him who purses her. (ISh, Sgh.) ― -b4- And AinoqaTaEa minohu saHoriY (tropical:) I despaired of him, or it. (A, K.) And A^anaA minohu gayoru Sariymi saHorK (tropical:) I am not in despair of him, or it. (A, B.) Sariymu saHorK is also expl. as signifying (tropical:) Having his hope cut off: and (tropical:) anything despaired of. (TA.) And Surima saHoruhu means (tropical:) His hope was cut off. (TA.) -A2- Also The scar of a gall on the back of a camel, (K, TA,) when it has healed, and the place thereof has become white. (TA.) -A3- And The upper, or highest, part of a valley. (TA.) -A4- See also saH~aArapN . -A5- And see saHarN , in two places.

definition: -A2- [Also] an inf.
sourceDefinition: : see saHorN , first sentence. -A2- [Also] an inf. n. of saHarahu , meaning (tropical:) The turning a thing from its proper manner of being to another manner: (T, TA: [accord. to the T, this seems to be proper; but accord. to the A, tropical:]) and hence, (T, TA,) (tropical:) enchantment, or fascination: (T, * S, * MA, KL, PS:) for when. the enchanter ( Als~aAHiru ) makes what is false to appear in the form of truth, and causes a thing to be imagined different from what it really is, it is as though he turned it from its proper manner of being: (T, TA:) the producing what is false in the form of truth: (IF, Msb:) or, in the common conventional language of the law, any event of which the cause is hidden, and which is imagined to be different from what it really is: and embellishment by falsification, and deceit: (Fakhred-Deen, Msb:) or a performance in which one allies himself to the devil, and which is effected by his aid: (TA:) i. q. A^axo*apN [meaning a kind of enchantment, or fascination, which captivates the eye and the like, and by which enchantresses withhold their husbands from other women ]: (S:) and anything of which the way of proceeding or operation ( maA^oxa*uhu ) is subtile: (S, K:) accord. to Ibn-Abee-'Áïsheh, siHor is thus called by the Arabs because it changes health, or soundness, to disease: (Sh:) [and in like manner it is said to change hatred to love: (see 1:)] pl. A^asoHaArN and suHuwrN . (TA.) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) Skilful eloquence: (TA:) or used absolutely, it is applied to that for which the agent is blamed: and when restricted, to that which is praiseworthy. (Msb.) Thus it is in the saying of Mohammad, A_in~a mina AlbayaAni lasiHorFA (tropical:) [ Verily there is a kind of eloquence that is enchantment ]: because the speaker propounds an obscure matter, and discloses its true meaning by the beauty of his eloquence, inclining the hearts [of his hearers] in like manner as they are inclined by siHor : or because there is in eloquence a novelty and strangeness of composition which attracts the hearer and brings him to such a pass as almost diverts him from other things; therefore it is likened to siHor properly so called: and it is said to be Als~iHoru AlHalaAlu [or lawful enchantment ]. (Msb.) The saying of Mohammad mentioned above was uttered on the following occasion: Keys Ibn-'Ásim El-Minkaree and EzZibrikán Ibn-Bedr and 'Amr Ibn-El-Ahtam came to the Prophet, who asked 'Amr respecting EzZibrikán; whereupon he spoke well of him: but Ez-Zibrikán was not content with this, and said, “ By God, O apostle of God, he knows that I am more excellent than he has said; but he envies the place that I have in thine estimation: ” and thereupon 'Amr spoke ill of him; and then said, “ By God, I did not lie of him in the first saying nor in the other; but he pleased me, and I spoke as pleased; then he angered me, and I spoke as angered: ” then Mohammad uttered the above-mentioned words. (TA.) Their meaning is, but God knows best, he praises the man, speaking truth respecting him, so as to turn the hearts of the hearers to him, (K,) or to what he says; (TA;) and he dispraises him, speaking truth respecting him, so as to turn their hearts also to him, (K,) or to what he says after. (TA.) A' Obeyd says nearly the same. Or, as some say, the meaning is, that there is an eloquence that is sinful like siHor . (TA.) ― -b3- Also (tropical:) Skill; science: Mohammad said, mano taEal~ama baAbFA mina Aln~ujuwmi faqado taEal~ama baAbFA mina Als~iHori (tropical:) [ He who learneth a process of the science of the stars (meaning astrology or astronomy) learneth a process of enchantment ], which may mean that the science of the stars is forbidden to be learned, like the science of enchantment, and that the learning of it is an act of infidelity: or it may mean that it is skill, and science; referring to what is acquired thereof by way of calculation; as the knowledge of eclipses of the sun or moon, and the like. (ISd, TA.) ― -b4- Also (tropical:) Food; aliment; nutriment: so called because its effect is subtile. (TA.) ― -b5- gayovN *uw siHorK means (assumed tropical:) Superabundant rain. (TA.)

definition: -A2- Also, (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: : see saHorN , in two places. -A2- Also, (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K, &c.,) and ↓ saHorN , (TA,) and ↓ suHurN , (Msb,) and ↓ saHariY~N , and ↓ saHariy~apN , (K,) (tropical:) The time a little before daybreak: (S, K:) or [simply] before daybreak: (Msb:) or the last part of the night: (Lth, Mgh:) or the last sixth of the night: (Mgh:) the pl. of saHarN (Msb) and of ↓ saHorN (TA) and of ↓ suHurN , (Msb,) is A^asoHaArN : (Msb, K, TA:) the saHar is thus met. called because it is the time of the departure of the night and the coming of the day; so that it is the mutanaf~as [lit. the “ time of the breathing, ” by which is meant the “ shining forth, ”] of the dawn: (A:) there are two times of which each is thus called; one, which is [specially] called Als~aHaru AlA^aEolaY , [or the earlier saHar ,] (A, Mgh,) is before daybreak; (Mgh;) or a little before daybreak: (A:) and the other, at daybreak: (A, Mgh:) like as one says “ the false dawn ” and “ the true: ” (A:) the earlier saHar is also called ↓ suHorapN : (S, K:) or the suHorap is the same as the saHar : or it is the last third of the night, to daybreak. (TA.) Using saHar indeterminately, you make it perfectly decl., and say, A^atayotuhu bisaHarK [ I came to him a little before daybreak ], agreeably with the phrase in the Kur liv. 34; (S;) and in like manner, ↓ bisuHorapK [ in the earlier saHar ]: (S, K:) you also say saHarFA , and ↓ suHorapF , (A,) and saHarFA mina AlA^asoHaAri : and maA zaAla EinodanaA muno*u Als~aHari [ He ceased not to be with us, or at our abode, from a little before daybreak ]: and laqiytuhu biAls~aHari AlA^aEolaY , and biA^aEolaY saHarayoni , and biA^aEolaY Als~aHarayoni , (TA,) and fiY A^aEolaY Als~aHarayoni , (A, TA,) [ I met him in the earlier saHar ;] but biA^aEolaY saHarK , a phrase used by El-'Ajjáj, is erroneous: (TA:) and h`*ihi All~ayolapi ↓ laqiytuhu saHariY~a and ↓ saHariy~atahaA [ I met him in the time a little before daybreak of this last night ]. (TA.) When, by saHar alone, you mean the saHar of the night immediately preceding, you say, laqiytuhu saHara yaA h`*aA [ I met him a little before daybreak this last night, O thou man], (S, K,) making it imperfectly decl. because it is altered from Als~aHara , (S,) or because it is for biAls~aHari ; (TA;) and it is thus determinate by itself, (S, K,) without its being prefixed to another noun and without Al : (S:) and in the same sense you say bisaHara : (TA:) and you say, siro EalaY farasika saHara yaA fataY [ Go thou on thy horse a little before daybreak this night, O youth: so in the TA; but in two copies of the S, for siro I find siyra ]: you do not make it to terminate with damm, [like qabolu and baEodu &c.,] because it is an adv. n. which, in a place where it is fitting to be such, may not be used otherwise than as such: (S:) and [in like manner] you say, ↓ laqiytuhu suHorapa yaA h`*aA [ I met him in the earlier saHar of this last night, O thou man]. (TA.) If you make saHar the proper name of a man, it is perfectly decl.: and so is the dim.; for it is not of the measure of a noun made to deviate from its original from, like A^uxaru : you say, ↓ siro EalaY farasika suHayorFA [ Go thou on thy horse a very little before daybreak: so in the TA; but here again, in two copies of the S, for siro I find siyra ]: you do not make it to terminate with damm, [like qabolu &c.,] because its being made of the dim. form does not bring it into the class of adv. ns. which may also be used as nouns absolutely, though it does bring it into the class of nouns which are perfectly declinable. (S, TA.) ― -b2- saHarN also signifies (tropical:) Whiteness overspreading blackness; (K;) like SaHarN ; except that the former is mostly used in relation to the time so called, of daybreak; and the latter, in relation to colours, as when one says HimaArN A^aSoHaru ; (TA;) and ↓ suHorapN signifies the same; (TA;) i. q. SuHorapN . (K.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) The extremity (T, A, K) of a desert, (T,) and of the earth or a land, (A,) or of anything: (K:) from the time of night so called: (A:) pl. A^asoHaArN . (T, A, K.)

Using saHar indeterminately, you make it perfectly decl., and say, A^atayotuhu bisaHarK [ I came to him a little before daybreak ], agreeably with the phrase in the Kur liv. 34; (S;) and in like manner, ↓ bisuHorapK [ in the earlier saHar ]: (S, K:) you also say saHarFA , and ↓ suHorapF , (A,) and saHarFA mina AlA^asoHaAri : and maA zaAla EinodanaA muno*u Als~aHari [ He ceased not to be with us, or at our abode, from a little before daybreak ]: and laqiytuhu biAls~aHari AlA^aEolaY , and biA^aEolaY saHarayoni , and biA^aEolaY Als~aHarayoni , (TA,) and fiY A^aEolaY Als~aHarayoni , (A, TA,) [ I met him in the earlier saHar ;] but biA^aEolaY saHarK , a phrase used by El-'Ajjáj, is erroneous: (TA:) and h`*ihi All~ayolapi ↓ laqiytuhu saHariY~a and ↓ saHariy~atahaA [ I met him in the time a little before daybreak of this last night ]. (TA.) When, by saHar alone, you mean the saHar of the night immediately preceding, you say, laqiytuhu saHara yaA h`*aA [ I met him a little before daybreak this last night, O thou man], (S, K,) making it imperfectly decl. because it is altered from Als~aHara , (S,) or because it is for biAls~aHari ; (TA;) and it is thus determinate by itself, (S, K,) without its being prefixed to another noun and without Al : (S:) and in the same sense you say bisaHara : (TA:) and you say, siro EalaY farasika saHara yaA fataY [ Go thou on thy horse a little before daybreak this night, O youth: so in the TA; but in two copies of the S, for siro I find siyra ]: you do not make it to terminate with damm, [like qabolu and baEodu &c.,] because it is an adv. n. which, in a place where it is fitting to be such, may not be used otherwise than as such: (S:) and [in like manner] you say, ↓ laqiytuhu suHorapa yaA h`*aA [ I met him in the earlier saHar of this last night, O thou man]. A^axoTaA^ahu . (M.) And Talabotuhumo fasarifotuhumo I sought them and missed them: or was ignorant of them. (Msb.) And sarifa Alqawoma He passed by the people, or party, and left them behind him. (M.) As relates, of an Arab of the desert, with whom some companions of his made an appointment to meet him in a certain place of the mosque, and to whom he broke his promise, that, being asked respecting that, he said, mararotu bikumo fasarifotukumo , meaning [ I passed by you and ] I was unmindful of you. (S.) And hence the saying of Jereer, (S, TA,) praising the Benoo-Umeiyeh, (TA,) A^aEoTawoA hunayodapa yaHoduwhaA vamaAniyapN maA fiY EaTaAy^ihimu min~N walaA sarafu meaning [ They gave a hundred camels, eight persons driving them, or urging them by singing to them: there was not in their gift reproach for a benefit conferred, nor ] unmindfulness: or the meaning is, nor missing ( xaTaA^N ); that is, they did not miss the proper place of the gift by their giving it to such as did not deserve it and refusing it to the deserving. (S, TA.) You say also, sarifotu yamiynahu I was unacquainted with, or knew not, his oath. (TA.) ― -b2- [ sarafN is also, as expl. below, syn. with A_isoraAfN , but as a subst., having no verb properly belonging to it.] -A2- sarafati Al$~ajarapa , (ISk, S, K,) aor. , inf. n. sarofN , (ISk, S,) said of the surofap [q. v.], It ate the leaves of the tree: (ISk, S, K:) and sarafati Alxa$aba is likewise said of the surofap [as meaning it ate the wood ]. (Z, TA.) And surifati Al$~ajarapu , (ISk, S, M, TA,) inf. n. sarofN , (ISk,) The tree had its leaves eaten by the surofap : (S:) or was smitten, or lighted on, by the surofap : (ISk, M, TA:) and sarifa Alxa$abu [ the wood was eaten by the surofap ], the verb in this phrase being quasi-pass. of the verb in the phrase sarafati Als~urofapu Alxa$ab~ , like as HaTima and SaEiqa are quasi-passives of the verbs in the phrases HaTamatohu Als~in~u and SaEaqatohu Als~amaA='u : (Z, TA:) and [hence] one says also, sarifa AlT~aEaAmu (tropical:) The wheat, or food, was, or became, cankered, or eaten away; as though smitten, or lighted on, by the surofap . (M, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence also,] surifato A^u*unu Al$~aApi (tropical:) The ear of the sheep, or goat, was entirely cut off. (A, TA.) ― -b3- And sarafato waladahaA (tropical:) She (a mother) injured her child by too much milk. (A, K, * TA.)

definition: , (Msb,) inf. n. A_isoraAfN , (M, Msb,) He exceeded, or transgressed, the just, or right, bound, or limit, or measure; acted extravagantly, exorbitantly, or immoderately: (M, Msb:) or A_isoraAfN...
sourceDefinition: , (Msb,) inf. n. A_isoraAfN , (M, Msb,) He exceeded, or transgressed, the just, or right, bound, or limit, or measure; acted extravagantly, exorbitantly, or immoderately: (M, Msb:) or A_isoraAfN signifies the being extravagant in expenditure, syn. tabo*iyrN ; (K) or so A_isoraAfN fiY Aln~afaqapi : (S, TA:) or, as some say, tb*yr means the “ exceeding in respect of the right objects of expenditure, ” which is ignorance of the [right] manner, and of things that should prevent it; and AsrAf means the exceeding with respect to quantity [ in expenditure ], and is ignorance of the values of the right objects: (MF in art. b*r :) or the latter signifies the expending otherwise than in obedience of God, (Sufyán, K, * TA,) whether little or much; (TA;) as also ↓ sarafN : (M, TA:) it is also said to mean the eating that which it is not lawful to eat; and this is said to be meant in the Kur vi. 142 or vii. 29: and the putting a thing in a wrong place [as when one expends his money upon a wrong object]: and accord. to Iyás Ibn-Mo'áwiyeh, AlA_isoraAfu is that [ action ] whereby one falls short of what is due to God. (TA.) You say also, Asrf fiY maAlihi , meaning He was hasty in respect of his property, [i. e. in expending it, ] without pursuing the just course, or keeping within due bounds. (M.) And Asrf fiY AlkalaAmi and fiY Alqatoli He exceeded the due bounds, or just limits, in speech, and in slaying. (M.) AlA_isoraAfu fiY Alqatoli , which is forbidden in the Kur xvii. 35, is said to mean The slaying of another than the slayer of one's companion: (Zj, M, Mgh: *) or the slaying the slayer without the authority of the Sultán: or the not being content with slaying one, but slaying a number of persons, because of the high rank of the slain and the low condition of the slayer: or the slaying one higher in rank than the slayer: (Zj, M:) or the slaying two when the slayer is one: or the maining or mutilating [ before slaughter ]. (Mgh.) A_isoraAfN also signifies The committing of many faults, offences, or crimes, and sins. (TA.) And you say, A^akalahu A_isoraAfFA (TA) and ↓ sarafFA , (M, TA,) meaning He ate it hastily. (M, TA.)

(S, M) of 'Áïsheh, (TA,) A_in~a lil~aHomi sarafFA kasarafi Alxamori [ Verily there is an addictedness to flesh-meat like the addictedness to wine ]: (S, M, TA:) i. e. he who is accustomed to it is addicted to the eating thereof, like as he who is constantly drinking wine is addicted thereto, having little selfrestraint therefrom: or the meaning here is unmindfulness [ of consequences with respect to flesh-meat &c.]: or corruptness of conduct, arising from hardness of heart, and daringness to disobey, and self-impulsion to the gratification of appetite: (TA:) or it may be [that the meaning is, there is an extravagance with respect to flesh-meat &c.,] from AlA_isoraAfu (S, TA) in expenditure for that which is not needed, or otherwise than in obedience [to the law of God]. The man shall not take a thing as spoil that is of high and great estimation, he being a believer ]: (K, TA:) [for] people disapprove of that: (TA:) and it is also related with $ [i. e. *At $arafK ]. (K.)

definition: [ A certain worm, or caterpillar, or small creeping thing;
sourceDefinition: [ A certain worm, or caterpillar, or small creeping thing; ] a small creeping thing that makes for itself a habitation, (S, K,) four-sided, or square, (S,) of fragments of wood, (S, K,) joining them together by means of its spittle, in the form of a naAw^uws [here meaning coffin ], (S,) which it then enters, and [ therein it ] dies: (S, K:) or the silkworm: or a certain small creeping thing, dust-coloured, that constructs a beautiful habitation in which it is: or a very small creeping thing, like the half of a lentil, that bores a tree, and then constructs therein a habitation of pieces of wood, which it conjoins by means of what resembles the web of the spider: or a very small dust-coloured creeping thing, that comes to a piece of wood and excavates it, and then brings a bit of wood and puts it therein, then another, then another, and then weaves what resembles the web of the spider: or, accord. to AHn, a certain small creeping thing, like the worm, inclining in some degree to blackness, found upon the [ plants called ] HamoD , that constructs a four-sided, or square, habitation, of pieces of wood, joining the extremities of these together by means of a thing [or substance ] resembling the web of the spider: or the worm [or caterpillar ] that weaves [a web ] upon certain trees, and eats their leaves, and destroys the rest thereof by that weaving: or a certain worm [or caterpillar ] like the finger, hairy, speckled with black or white, that eats the leaves of trees so as to make them bare: or a certain worm [or caterpillar ] that weaves upon itself, of the size of the finger in length, a thing like the qiroTaAs [or roll, or scroll, of paper ], which it enters, so becoming unattainable: or a certain light, small creeping thing, like a spider: (M:) pl. surafN . (TA.) Hence the prov., A^aSonaEu mino surofapK [ More skilled in fabricating than a surofap ]. (S, M, K.) And one says also, A^axaf~u mino surofapK [ Lighter than a surofap ]. (M.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. saqabN , He, or it, was, or became, near. (Msb.) saqabN is syn. with qurobN . (S, A, K.) You say, saqibato daAruhu , (S, and so in the K accord. to the TA,) with kesr [to the q ], (S,) [inf. n. as above;] or saqabat , (so in the CK and in my MS. copy of the K and in my copy of the Mgh,) inf. n. saqobN , (so in my copy of the Mgh,) or suquwbN ; (K;) [but I believe the verb to be correctly saqibat , like its syn. Saqibat , and the inf. n. to be correctly saqabN , and perhaps suquwbN also;] His house was near; (S, Mgh, K;) as also ↓ A^asoqabat . (S, K.) It is said in a trad., AljaAru A^aHaq~u bisaqabihi , meaning [ The neighbour has a better, or the best, claim to pre-emption] by reason of his being near: (S, * A, Msb:) or the b is a connective of AHq~ with its complement, (Mgh, Msb,) not to denote a cause, (Mgh,) and bisaqabihi is expl. as meaning biAl$~ufoEapi ; (Mgh, Msb;) i. e. the neighbour has a better, or the best, claim to Al$~ufoEap [or pre-emption ], when his house is contiguous: (Mgh:) IAth says that it is adduced as an evidence that Al$~ufoEap belongs to the neighbour though not a sharer; i. e., that he has a better claim thereto than one who is not a neighbour: but some explain AljAr as meaning the partner, or sharer: or the meaning of the trad. may be, the neighbour has a better, or the best, claim to kindness and assistance because of his being near. (L, TA. [See also another reading ( biSaqabihi ), and explanations thereof, in art. Sqb .])

definition: The young one of a camel: or, when just brought forth: (K:) or only the male young one of a camel: (S, K:) [see also SaqobN :] when a she-camel has brought forth her young one, the latter, when just...
sourceDefinition: The young one of a camel: or, when just brought forth: (K:) or only the male young one of a camel: (S, K:) [see also SaqobN :] when a she-camel has brought forth her young one, the latter, when just born, is called saliylN , before it is known whether it is a male or a female; but when it is known, if it is a male, it is called saqobN : (As, TA:) the female is not called saqobapN , (S, K,) but HaAy^ilN : (S:) or it is [sometimes] called by the former of these appellations: (K:) [see De Sacy's Chrest. Arabe, 2nd ed., ii. 358: and see saqobapN below:] the pl. is A^asoqubN [a pl. of pauc.] and siqaAbN and suquwbN and suqobaAnN . (K.) A^a*al~u mina Als~uqobaAni bayona AlHalaAy^ibi [ More vile than the male young ones of camels among the milch camels ] is a prov. [from a verse of Keys Ibn-El-Khateem]. (TA.) ― -b2- Tall: (K: [see also sakobN :]) or anything tall, together with plumpness; or fatness, softness, thinness of the skin, and plumpness. (S.
