definition: Strength, might, force, or power;
sourceDefinition: Strength, might, force, or power; (TA;) as also ↓ saloTanapN : (Bd in iii. 144:) predominance; the possession, or exercise, of superior power or force, or of dominion, or authority, and power, or of absolute dominion or authority and power; (Mgh;) as also ↓ suloTapN ; (S;) the former being syn. with tasal~uTN [used as a subst.]; (Mgh;) and the latter being the subst. from tasal~aTa : (S:) power of dominion; sovereign, or ruling, power; (M;) [in this sense, as well as in the first,] i. q. ↓ saloTanapN ; (Msb;) power of a king; (Lth, Mgh, K;) and of a governor; (Mgh, Msb;) [i. e.] delegated power, or power given to one who is not a king; (TA;) also written suloTaAnN ; (M, Msb, K;) which is the only instance of this form: (Msb:) it is masc. and fem.; (M, TA;) generally masc., in the opinion of the skilful; but sometimes fem.; so say IAmb and Zj and others: (Msb:) but ISk says that it is fem. (TA.) One says, (ISk,) or some say, (Msb,) qaDato bihi Als~uloTaAnu (ISk, Msb) The sovereign, or ruling, power (↓ Als~aloTanapu ) decreed it. (Msb.) And Aboo-Zuheyr says, I heard one, in whose chasteness of speech I have confidence, say, A^atatonaA suloTaAnN jaAy^irapN [ A tyrannical sovereign, or ruling, power, came to us ]. (Msb.) It is said in a trad., A_il~aA A^ano tasoA^ala *aA suloTaAnK , meaning Unless thou ask the ruler, or governor, or the king, for thy due from the public treasury. (Mgh.) And you say, qado jaEalotu laka suloTaAnFA EalaY A^axo*i Haq~iY mino fulaAnK I have given thee power, or authority, to take, or receive, my due from such a one. (TA.) And laA yaw^um~u Alr~ajulu Alr~ajula fiY suloTaAnihi [ A man shall not take precedence of a man in his authority ]; meaning, in his house, and where he has predominance, or superior power, or authority; nor shall he sit upon his cushion; for in doing so he would show him contempt. (Mgh.) ― -b2- Strength, or hardness, of anything: (M, K:) sharpness of anything: force, or violence, of anything. (TA.) The vehemence of winter. (TK.) An excited and predominant state of the blood; or inflammation thereof. (IDrd, M, K.) The flaming, or blazing, of fire. (IDrd.) ― -b3- A proof; an evidence; an argument; a plea; an allegation; syn. Huj~apN , (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) and burohaAnN : (S, Msb:) a Huj~ap being thus called because of the force with which truth attacks the mind: (B:) or, accord. to Mohammad Ibn-Yezeed, from saliyTN , (M, TA,) signifying “ oil of olives, ” because it enlightens: (TA:) and in these senses it has no pl., because it is used in the place of an inf. n. (S, TA.) Accord. to I'Ab, it signifies Huj~ap wherever it occurs in the Kur. (TA.) But in the words of the Kur [xvii. 35], faqado jaEalonaA liwal~iyihi suloTaAnFA , the meaning may be either [ We have given to his executor, or heir, ] authority, and power, or absolute authority and power, or the like; or a plea, or the like. (Mgh.) And again, in the Kur [lxix. 29], halaka Ean~iY suloTaAniyaho , the meaning may be My dominion, and my authority and power over men, has perished from me; or my plea. (Bd, B.) And sometimes it means A miracle; as in the words of the Kur [li. 38], A_i*o A^arosalonaAhu A_ilaY firoEawona bisuloTaAn K mubiynK [ When we sent him to Pharaoh with a manifest miracle ]. (TA.) Az says that it is sometimes masc. because it has a masc. form; and thus it is in the last of the instances above. (TA.) ― -b4- Also A ruler, or governor, or the like; a king; a sovereign; (S, K, TA;) a khaleefeh: (TA:) these are its most common applications [in the writings of post-classical times]: (TA:) thus applied because the person so called is made to predominate; to have, or exercise, superior power or force; to have dominion, or the like: or because he is one of the evidences of God: (Aboo-Bekr, TA:) or because he possesses proof or evidence [of his right]: or because by him pleas and rights are established: (TA:) or because he enlightens the earth, (Msb, * B,) and is of great usefulness; (B;) the word being derived from saliyTN [signifying “ olive-oil ”]: (Msb:) it is of the measure fuEolaAnN : (S:) and when [thus] applied to a person, it is masc.: (Msb:) or it is masc. and fem.: (S, TA:) accord. to Mohammad Ibn-Yezeed, (TA,) fem. because it is [originally] pl. of saliyTN applied to “ oil; ” as though the kingdom shone by him; or because it has the signification of Huj~apN : and sometimes masc., because regarded as meaning a man; (K, TA;) or because regarded as a sing.: so says Mohammad Ibn-Yezeed; but Az observes that none beside him says this: Fr says that he who makes it masc. regards it as meaning rajulN ; and he who makes it fem. regards it as meaning Huj~apN : (TA:) the pl. is salaATiynu . definition: Strong, or hard;
sourceDefinition: Strong, or hard; (M, K;) as also ↓ saliTN , (M,) or ↓ saloTN . (K.) You say, ↓ HaAfirN saliTN , (M,) or ↓ saloTN , (TA,) and saliyTN , (M, TA,) A strong, or hard, solid hoof. (M, TA.) And AlHaAfiri ↓ daAb~apN saliTapu A beast having a strong, or hard, hoof. (M.) And Alxuf~i ↓ baEiyrN saliTu A camel having a strong, or hard, foot. (M.) ― -b2- Sharp; applied to anything. (K.) You say also ↓ sanaAbiku saliTaAtN Sharp edges of the fore parts of hoofs. (S, TA.) ― -b3- Chaste in speech, or eloquent, (S, K,) and sharp in tongue: (S:) an epithet of praise when applied to the male, and of dispraise when [with p ] applied to the female: (IDrd, K:) also, (K,) long-tongued; (M, K;) and so ↓ saliTN , (M,) or ↓ saloTN ; (K;) fem. saliyTapN , and ↓ salaTaAnapN , (M, K,) and ↓ siliTaAnapN , (K,) or ↓ siliT~aAnapN ; (M;) the last written [thus] with tesh-deed to the T in the Jm., and there explained as signifying long-tongued and clamorous: (TA:) or saliyTN signifies clamorous and foul-tongued; and so saliyTapN applied to a woman: (Msb:) or the latter, applied to a woman, clamorous: (S:) or long-tongued and vehemently clamorous: (Lth:) or saliyTapu All~isaAni is applied to a woman in two senses; signifying sharp-tongued; and long-tongued. (Msb, K.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. samaAHN and samaAHapN and sumuwHN and sumuwHapN and samoHN and simaAHN , (K,) He was, or became, liberal, bountiful, munificent, or generous; (S, * Msb, * K;) as also ↓ AsmH : (Msb, K:) but the unaugmented verb commonly known, but faultily omitted in the K, is samaHa , aor. ; and this is the only one mentioned by IKtt and IKoot and a number of other authors: samuHa , like karuma , means he became of the people of Als~amaAHap [i. e. liberality, &c.]: (MF:) [but] samaHa and ↓ AsmH both signify as above; he was, or became, liberal, &c.; and he gave from a motive of generosity and liberality: this is the correct explanation of both; though some say that the former only is used in this sense; and the latter, in relation to compliance and submissiveness. (L.) You say, samaHa bihi , (S, A, Msb,) aor. , inf. n. samaAHN and samaAHapN (S, * A, * Msb) and sumuwHN , (Msb,) He was liberal, bountiful, munificent, or generous, with it; (S, A, Msb;) and gave it; and complied therein with that which was desired of him; as also ↓ AsmH . (Msb.) [And samaHa lahu He was liberal, &c., to him; as also ↓ AsmH ; whence,] God is represented, in a trad., as saying, liEabodiY ↓ A^asomiHuwA kaA_isomaAHihi A_ilaY EibaAdiY Be ye liberal, &c., to my servant, [meaning Mohammad,] like as he is liberal, &c., to my servants. (L.) And samaHa liY , (S,) or lahu , (A,) He gave (S, A) to me, (S,) or to him: (A:) and bika*aA ↓ saAmaHahu he gave him such a thing. (Msb.) And samaHa liY bi*`lika , and ↓ AsmH , and ↓ sAmH , He complied with my desire in that thing. (L: see also a similar phrase below.) ― -b2- samaHato , said of a she-camel, means She became submissive, and went quickly: (L:) and ↓ AsmHt said of a beast ( daAb~ap ), it became gentle and submissive after being refractory: (L, K: *) and in like manner ↓ AsmH ; (A;) and ↓ sm~H , inf. n. tasomiyHN ; (L;) said of a camel: (A, L:) or tasomiyHN signifies the going an easy pace: (S, L, K:) and the going quickly: (L, K:) or (so in the L, but in the K “ and ”) the act of fleeing. (L, K.) And ↓ AsmH It became easy and submissive. (L.) You say, qaruwnatuhu ↓ A^asomaHato , (S, A, K,) and qariynatuhu , as also ↓ saAmaHato , (L,) His mind became submissive, (S, A, L, K,) li*`lika AlA^amori to that thing. (L.) ― -b3- samaHa , inf. n. samaAHN ; (L;) and ↓ sm~H , (Mgh, L,) inf. n. tasomiyHN ; (L, K;) and ↓ sAmH , (Mgh, L,) inf. n. musaAmaHapN ; (S, A, L, K;) and ↓ AsmH , (Mgh,) and ↓ tsm~H ; (L;) also signify He acted in an easy, or a gentle, manner; (S, A, Mgh, L, K;) and he made easy, or facilitated; (L;) fiY A^amorK in an affair: (Mgh, L:) and ↓ musaAmaHapN signifies the acting in an easy, or a gentle, manner in a contest in thrusting, or piercing, with spears or the like, and smiting with swords, and running. (L.) It is said in a well-known trad., Als~amaAHu rabaAHN The acting in an easy, or a gentle, manner, in affairs, is a means of gain, or profit, to the performer thereof. (L.) And you say, fiY AlA^amori ↓ sAmHhu He acted in an easy, or a gentle, manner with him. (TK.) And samaHa lahu and bihi , and ↓ AsmH , He made [a thing] easy to him. (L.) And AisomaHo yusomaHo laka (Meyd, Mgh, L) and bika , (L,) and yusomaHo laka ↓ A^asomiHo (Meyd, L) and bika , (L,) a trad., (Mgh, L,) meaning Facilitate thou, and facilitation shall be rendered to thee: (As, Sh, L:) or act thou in an easy, or a gentle, manner, and easy, or gentle, treatment, shall be rendered to thee: (Mgh:) or be thou compliant, and compliance shall be rendered to thee. (Meyd.) And samaHa lahu biHaAjatihi , and ↓ AsmH , He made easy to him the object of his want. (IAar, L: see also a similar phrase above.) ― -b4- samaAHapN (A, TA) and sumuwHapN , (TA,) [app. inf. ns. of which the verb is samuHa ,] in a branch, or rod, signify (tropical:) The being even and smooth, without any knots [or inequality of thickness: see samoHN ]. (A, TA.)

definition: (tropical:) They made him, or appointed him, ruler, or governor, over them;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) They made him, or appointed him, ruler, or governor, over them; (M, * TA;) as also ↓ AsAswhu . (TA.) ― -b2- suw~isa Alr~ajulu A^umuwra Aln~aAsi , (S, K,) or A^amora Aln~aAsi , (as in the TA,) or A^amora qawomihi , (A,) (tropical:) The man was made ruler of the affairs of the people; (S;) [or of the affairs of his people, accord. as the phrase is given in the A:] or was made king. (K.) Accord. to a relation of a verse of El-Hotei-ah, he uses the expression saw~asota A^mora baniyka [as though meaning Thou hast ruled the affairs of thy sons ]; but Fr says that saw~asota is a mistake. (S. [Thus I find it in one copy of the S: but in another copy of the S, I find saw~asoti , which is clearly wrong; and in the TA, suw~isota , which Fr can hardly be supposed to have disallowed.]) ― -b3- saw~asa lahu A^amorFA (assumed tropical:) He made an affair easy to him; syn. ruw~aDahu and *al~alahu . (TA.) (AZ, K. *) ― -b4- sw~s AlmaroA^apa He slit the vulva of the woman. (TA.) -A2- See also 1, in two places.

definition: [The grub, or larva of the phalæna tinea and of the curculio;
sourceDefinition: [The grub, or larva of the phalæna tinea and of the curculio; i. e. the moth-worm and the weevil; ] the kind of worm that attacks wool (S, A, K) and cloths (TA) and wheat or other food: (S, TA:) and with p , [a n. un.,] i. q. Euv~apN ; (Mgh, Msb;) as also ↓ saAsN ; (TA;) i. e., a worm that attacks wool and cloths (Mgh, Msb) and wheat or other food: (Mgh:) and suwsN , the kind of worm (M, Msb) called Euv~N , (M,) that eats grain (M, Msb) and wood: (Msb:) n. un. with p : (M, Msb:) and any eater of a thing is termed suwsuhu , whether worm or other thing. (M.) One says, AlEiyaAlu suwsu AlmaAli (assumed tropical:) [ The persons who compose a household are the grubs of property ]: i. e., they consume it by little and little like as suws consume grain, which can scarcely be cleared of them when they attack it. (Msb.) -A2- [The licoriceplant; so called in the present day;] a kind of tree, (AHn, M, K,) or plant, (Mgh,) well known, (Mgh, K,) with which houses are covered above the roofs, (AHn, M, Mgh,) the expressed juice of which is an ingredient in medicine, (AHn, M,) the leaves of which are put into [ the beverage called ] nabiy* , and make it strong like [ the strong drink called ] daA*iY~ , (Mgh,) in the roots of which is sweetness (AHn, M, K) intense in degree, (AHn, M,) and in its branches is bitterness, (AHn, M, K,) and it abounds in the countries of the Arabs: (AHn, M:) or a kind of tree that grows in leaves without twigs: (M:) or a certain herb resembling [ the species of trefoil called ] qat~ . (TA.) [The root is vulgarly called, in the present day, Eiroq suws : and so is a strong infusion prepared from it, which is a very pleasant drink: and its inspissated juice is called rub~ Als~uws .] -A3- Nature; natural disposition: (S, M, A, K:) and origin. (S, A, K.) One says, AlfaSaAHapu mino suwsihi (S, M) Chasteness of speech, or eloquence, is [a quality] of his nature. (S.) And Alkaramu mino suwsihi (Lh, M, A) Generosity is [a quality] of his nature. (A.) And fulaAnN mino suwsi SidoqK Such a one is of good origin. (S.)

definition: Pieces of wood, (T, Msb, K,) bound together [ at the top ], upon which clothes are spread, (T, Msb,) or upon which clothes are put;
sourceDefinition: Pieces of wood, (T, Msb, K,) bound together [ at the top ], upon which clothes are spread, (T, Msb,) or upon which clothes are put; as also ↓ $ijaAbN ; (K;) of which latter the pl. is $ujubN : (TA: [see this last word above:]) pieces of wood, or sticks, of which the heads are joined together, and the feet parted asunder, upon which clothes are put, and sometimes the water-skins are hung thereon for the purpose of cooling the water: (Nh, TA:) or a piece of wood upon which clothes are put: (S:) Suh says, in the R, that they used to call the water-skin $ajobN , and they used not to hold it otherwise than suspended, so that mi$ojabN properly signifies the piece of wood, or stick, to which the water-skin is suspended: then they amplified the application of this word so as to call thereby the thing upon which clothes are suspended: (MF, TA:) the pl. is ma$aAjibu . (A.)

sourceDefinition: , (K, TA,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. $aTobN , (AZ, TA,) He cut (K, TA) into oblong pieces, or strips, flesh-meat, and a camel's hump, and a hide, or leather: (TA:) or he cut into strips, but without separating them, a camel's hump. (AZ, TA.) ― -b2- And $aTabati Aljariyda , [aor. ,] inf. n. $aTobN , She (a woman) split the palm-sticks, or palmbranches stripped of their leaves, to make of them mats: which being done, says A'Obeyd, [or when they have been peeled,] the $aATibap [q.v.] throws them to the munaq~iyap . (S.) [Or] $aTabat , aor. , inf. n. $uTuwbN , She removed the upper peel of the $aTob , or [ fresh, green ] palm-branches. (ISk, TA.) -A2- $aTaba also signifies It inclined, or declined, turned aside or away, deflected, or deviated, and became distant, or remote; (As, O, K;) and so $aTafa ; and both signify it went away. (As, TA.) One says, $aTaba Eanohu It turned aside or away, and became distant, or remote, from him, or it. (K.) Thus, in a trad., $aTaba Alr~umoHu Eano maqotalihi The spear deflected from, and failed to reach, his vital part. (O, TA. *) And one says also, $aTabati Ald~aAru The dwelling was, or became, distant, or remote. (O.)

sourceDefinition: pl. of ↓ $aTobapN , (S, Msb,) [or rather a coll. gen. n., of which the latter is the n. un.,] like as tamorN is of tamorapN ; (Msb;) Fresh, (A,) or green, (Msb,) or green and fresh, (S, K,) palm-branches (S, A, Msb, K) stripped of their leaves: (A:) or they are less than what are termed $aTaAy^ibu , of which the sing. is ↓ $aTiybapN ; and the $TAy^b are less than the karaAniyf : [i. e. the kironaAf is the thickest part of the palm-branch; next is the $aTiybap ; and next to this, the $aTobap :] or ↓ $aTobapN signifies a green palm-branch. (K.) kamasal~i ↓ $aTobapK , in a trad. of Umm-Zara, [as expl. in art. sl , q. v.,] means Like a green palm-stick drawn forth from its skin: or like a sword drawn forth [from its scabbard]: (TA in art. sl :) [for] ― -b2- ↓ $aTobapN signifies also A sword. (Aboo-Sa'eed, K.) ― -b3- [Hence, app.,] $aTobN is used also as an epithet, meaning (tropical:) Tall, and well made; (A, K, TA;) applied to a man and to a horse. (TA.) And, applied to a boy, or young man, (tropical:) Plump; or fat, soft, thin-skinned, and plump: and so ↓ $aTobapN applied to a girl, or young woman: (A:) or the former, applied to a boy, or young man, well made, and neither tall nor short: (TA:) or, so applied, light, or active, in body, and sharpheaded: (IAar, TA in art. EDb , voce EaDobN :) or it means, so applied, long and even ( sabiTN ) in the bones, light of flesh; likened to the palm-stick that is split: but this epithet is mostly used with p , i. e. ↓ $aTobapN , which is applied to a mare: (Ham p. 298:) or this epithet, $aTobapN , applied to a mare, means lank ( sabiTapN ) in flesh; (K, TA;) or tall; (TA;) as also ↓ $iTobapN in the former sense, (K, TA,) or in the latter; and the masc. is not thus used, applied to a horse: (TA:) and ↓ $aTobapN , (S,) or ↓ $iTobapN , (K,) or both, but the former is the more approved, (TA,) beautiful; plump; or fat, soft, thin-skinned, and plump; (K, TA;) and tall: (K:) or simply tall; (S, TA;) as also ↓ ma$oTuwbN and ↓ mu$aT~abN applied to a man. (TA.)

definition: The inf. n. $agorN , accord. to Ibn-Nubáteh, primarily signifies The raising the leg or hind leg, without restriction; and then by a metaphorical usage, the doing so for the purpose of copulation,...
sourceDefinition: The inf. n. $agorN , accord. to Ibn-Nubáteh, primarily signifies The raising the leg or hind leg, without restriction; and then by a metaphorical usage, the doing so for the purpose of copulation, and for making water: but the explanations of J [and of Z in the A] and of Fei and of F are at variance with his assertion. (MF.) [Accord. to these authorities,] $agara , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. as above, (Msb, TA,) signifies He (a dog) raised one of his hind legs (S, A, Msb, K) to make water, (S, Msb,) or and made water, or whether he made water or did not: (A, K:) and $agara birijolihi he (a dog) raised his hind leg, and made water. (TA.) And $agarato She (a camel) raised her hind leg, and struck [ with it, or kicked, ] the young one. (A.) And, said of a woman, (Msb, K,) She raised her leg, (Msb, and so in some copies of the K,) or her legs, (so in other copies of the K,) for the purpose of copulation. (Msb, K.) And the verb is also trans.: you say, $agara AlmaroA^apa , (Msb, K,) inf. n. $uguwrN , (K, [but this is a strange form in the case of a trans. verb,]) He raised the woman's leg, (Msb, and so in some copies of the K) or legs, (IDrd, O, and so in some copies of the K,) for the purpose of copulation; and so ↓ A$grhA . (IDrd, O, Msb, K.) And $agorN as the act of a stallion [camel] signifies His striking with his head beneath the she-camel, at the part next the udder, and so raising her, and throwing her down [app. for the purpose of copulation ]. (K.) ― -b2- $agarotu birijoliY fiY Algariybi means (assumed tropical:) I overcame the people in guarding, or protecting, the stranger. (AA, O, K.) ― -b3- And $agorN signifies also (assumed tropical:) The being distant, or remote. (Fr, K.) One says, $agara Albaladu , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , inf. n. $uguwrN , (Msb, [accord. to the K, app., $agorN ,]) (assumed tropical:) The country, or town, was, or became, remote from him who should aid it against the enemy, and him who should exercise sovereign sway, (K, TA,) and from him who should manage its affairs with prudence, precaution, or sound judgment: (TA:) or destitute of a guardian, or protector, to defend it: (Msb:) or destitute of people: [and so, app., $agara Albaladu birijolihi ; for it is immediately added,] one says balodapN $aAgirapN birijolihaA meaning as expl. below: (S:) and $agarati AlA^aroDu the land had not remaining in it any one to defend it, and to manage its affairs with prudence, precaution, or sound judgment. (K.) -A2- Also, i. e. $agorN , The making [another, or others,] to go forth [from a place]. (K.) One says, $agarotuhu Eani AlA^aroDi I made him to go forth from the land: (AA, TA:) and $agarotu baniY fulaAnK mino mawoDiEi ka*aA I made the sons of such a one to go forth from such a place: (S:) or $agaruwA fulaAnFA Eano baladihi They drove away, expelled, or banished. such a one from his country, or town; and the inf. n. is $agorN and $igaArN . (TA.) ― -b2- And i. q. taforiqapN [The act of scattering, or dispersing ]. (K.)

definition: , (Mgh, Msb, K,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. $igaArN , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) He gave him in marriage a woman on the condition of his giving him in marriage another, without dowry [ from either ]; concubitus with each of the said women being [ in lieu of ] the dowry for the other: or it applies peculiarly to female relations [ of the men so contracting ]; (K;) so that the meaning is only he gave him in marriage his female relation on the condition of his doing the like to him: (TA:) or he gave him in marriage a female under his guardianship, the other man doing to him the like, on the condition that concubitus with each one of the said females should be [ in lieu of ] the dowry for the other: (Mgh, * Msb:) or he gave him in marriage his sister on the condition of receiving in marriage the other's sister, without any dowry beside this: (A:) or he said to him, Give me in marriage thy daughter, or thy sister, on the condition of my giving thee in marriage my daughter, or my sister, concubitus with each one of the said females being [ in lieu of ] the dowry of the other. (S.) The practice of $igaAr was common in the Time of Ignorance, (Msb,) but is forbidden to the Muslims. (S, A.) ― -b2- $igaArN also signifies Two men's going forth into the field from two armies, and, when one of them has almost overcome his fellow, two men's coming to aid one of them, whereupon the other cries out, laA $igaAra laA $igaAra : (TA:) or two men's acting wrongfully, or injuriously, towards another man: (K, TA:) thus expl. by ISd. (TA.) And The acting with enmity, or hostility. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, O,) or yaduhu , (Mgh, TA,) or Alyadu , (Msb, K,) originally $alilato , (Mgh, Msb, TA,) aor. ta$al~u , (S, O, &c.,) inf. n. $alalN (S, * O, * Mgh, Msb, K) and $al~N , (Msb, K,) or the latter is not allowable; (Ham p. 69;) this is the chaste form of the verb; (Th, TA;) and ↓ A^u$il~ato ; (Th, K;) and $ul~ato , (Th, O, K,) but this last is bad, (Th, O, TA,) and is disallowed by Fr; (TA;) His right hand or arm, or his hand or arm, or the hand or arm, was, or became, unsound, or vitiated: (S, O, TA:) or deprived of the power of motion by an unsound, or a vitiated, state of its Euruwq [meaning veins or nerves ]: (Msb:) or dried up; or stiff: or it went [or wasted ] away. (K, TA.) One says, in praying for a person, laA ta$olalo yaduka [ May thy hand, or arm, not become unsound, &c.]: (S, Msb, * K: *) and laA $alalFA and ↓ laA $alaAli , which mean the same; the last word like qaTaAmi . (K.) And $al~a Ea$oruhu , and xamosuhu , [ His ten fingers became unsound, &c., and his five fingers,] and some say $al~ato , but this is more rare; i. e., the suppression of the fem. t is more usual in a case of this kind. (Lh, TA.) To one who has shot or thrown, or who has pierced or thrust, well, one says, laA $alalFA walaA EamFY [Mayest thou not experience unsoundness, &c., nor blindness ]; and laA $al~a Ea$oruka [ May thy ten fingers not become unsound, &c.], meaning A^aSaAbiEuka . (S, O.) He who says $al~a AlmaArinu and $al~ati AlA^u*unu is a foreigner. (Mgh.) The lawyers [improperly] use Al$~alal in relation to the *akar . (Msb.) One says also, $alilota yaA rajulu [ Thou hast become unsound, &c., in thy hand or thine arm, O man ]. (S, O.) And laA $alala , meaning laA ta$olalo , because it occupies the place of an imperative. (Lth, TA.) In the saying of the rájiz, (S,) namely, Abu-l-Khudree El-Yarboo'ee, (O, TA,) muhora A^abiY AljaboHaAbi laA ta$al~iY [ Colt of Abu-l-Habháb, mayest thou not become unsound , &c., in the fore leg], (S, TA, [in the O, AbY AlHarivi , for AbY AlH`rivi ,]) the last word is thus [for lA ta$olalo ] on account of the rhyme: (S, O, TA:) [for] the next hemistich is baAraka fiyka A@ll~`hu mino *iY A^al~i [ God bless thee as one possessing fleetness, or swiftness ]; (O, TA;) *Y Al~ in this instance meaning *Y suroEapK . (S in art. Al .) -A2- $al~ahu ; (K;) and $alalotu AlA_ibila , (S, O,) and Alr~ajula ; (Msb;) aor. , (S, Msb,) inf. n. $al~N (S, O, Msb, K *) and $alalN , (K, * and Ksh in xii. 3,) like as qaSaSN is inf. n. of qaS~a , (Ksh ibid.,) or $alalN is a simple subst.; (S, O;) He drove him away; (K;) and I drove away (S, O, Msb) the camels, (S, O,) and the man. (TA.) ― -b3- And $al~ati AlEayonu damoEahaA (assumed tropical:) The eye sent forth [or shed ] its tears: (Lh, K:) like $an~atohu : (Lh, TA:) asserted by Yaa- koob to be formed by substitution [of l for n ]. (O, TA.) ― -b5- $alalotu Alv~awoba , (S, O, Msb, TA,) inf. n. $al~N , (O,) I sewed the garment, or piece of cloth, (S, O, Msb, TA,) slightly; (S, O, TA; [omitted, probably by inadvertence, in my copy of the Msb;]) [previously to the second sewing termed Alkaf~u ;] strangely omitted in the K: ↓ $ilaAlapN is [app. a subst., not an inf. n., signifying The act, or art, of so sewing; ] the contr. of kifaAfapN . sourceDefinition: A heat; a single run, or a run at once, to a goal, or limit; (Mgh, Msb, K;) syn. TalaqN : (S, Msb:) pl. A^a$owaATN . (S, Mgh, Msb, K.) You say, EadaA $awoTFA He ran a heat. (S.) And TaAfa baAlbayoti saboEapa A^a$owaATK He performed seven circuits round the House [of God, i. e. the Kaabeh]: (S, TA:) from the [Black] Stone to the [Black] Stone [again] is one $awoT : (S, Msb, TA:) but some of the lawyers disapprove of this application of the term A$wAT . (IF, K, TA.) ― -b2- [It is also, app., an inf. n. used as an epithet: for one says, jaA='a $awoTN mina Alxayoli : see sananN , in the latter part of the paragraph.] It is sometimes used in relation to the wind: so says Lth: and he cites the following as an instance in which the wind is meant: wanaAziHK muEotakiri AlA^a$owaATi [app. meaning And a wind, or many a wind, exhausting, or drying up, the waters, the blasts thereof bringing dust ]. (TA.) ― -b3- And it is also [used as meaning A bout ] of shooting arrows. (T and M in art. r$q .) ― -b4- Also The space of ground over which a horse runs; such as a mayodaAn , and the like; which is [said by some to be] the primary signification; [but the primary signification is said by others to be the first given above; (see Har p. 574;)] and so ↓ ta$owiyTapN . (TA.) ― -b5- Also (assumed tropical:) A scope; an object to be reached, or accomplished; syn. gaAyapN : whence the saying, Al$~awoTu baTiynN (assumed tropical:) The scope is remote: (Har p. 574:) a prov., relating to the long extent of hope. (TA.) ― -b6- And (assumed tropical:) A place between two elevated tracts of ground, through which water and men pass, as though it were a road, extending as far as the voice of a caller can be heard, then ending, (ISh, O, K,) of such depth that it will conceal the camel and his rider, found only in plain, or soft, ground, and producing good herbage: (ISh, O:) pl. $iyaATN ; (ISh, O, K;) originally $iwaATN . (ISh, O.) Z writes it with s . (TA. See sawoTN .) -A2- $awoTu baraAHK i. q. Aibonu A=waY [ The jackal ]: (IDrd, S, Z, O, L, K:) or some other beast. (L.) -A3- $awoTu baATilK : see sawoTu baATilK , in art. swT : accord. to IDrd, it is not of established authority. (O.)

A_i$aAHapN , (IAar, TA,) He was cautious, or in fear, (S, A, K,) minohu [ of it ], (A, TA,) i. e. a thing, or an affair, (TA,) and EalaY HaAjatihi [ for the thing that he wanted ]; (K;) as also ↓ $AyH , (S, A, K,) inf. mu$aAyaHapN and $iyaAHN ; and ↓ $aAHa : (K:) or he was cautious and in fear, endeavouring to repel death. (L.) ― -b2- But in the dial. of Hudheyl, (S,) He strove, laboured, toiled, or exerted himself, fiY A^amorK [ in an affair ]; and so ↓ $AyH . (S, A.) ― -b3- And He continued journeying, or going on. (O.) ― -b4- A$AH biwajohihi He turned away his face, (S, A, TA,) from a [person or] thing, or from the heat of fire, or a hot odour, and from something hurtful: (TA:) or he exerted himself in aversion or turning away. (IAar, TA.) One says, kal~amotuhu faA^a$aAHa biwajohihi I spoke to him, and he turned away his face. (A.) ― -b5- A$AH also signifies He advanced, or came forward; syn. A^aqobala . (Fr, O, TA.) [Thus it has two contr. meanings. See also the part. n., mu$iyHN .] ― -b6- And He defended what was behind his back. (IAth, TA.) [See, again, the part. n.] ― -b7- A$AH bi*anabihi , said of a horse, He let his tail hang down loosely. (Lth, S.) (S.) ↓ Sabiy~apN signifies A young woman, girl, or female child; (S, TA;) and so too, [sometimes,] SabiY~N : (TA:) and the pl. is SabaAyaA . (S TA.) ― -b2- A^um~u AlS~iboyaAni is a term applied to The flatus, or flatulence, ( Alr~iyHu ,) that is incident to children. (TA in art. Am .) [Golius, in that art., explains it as meaning Larva, terriculamentum puerorum; on the authority of Meyd.: and also as meaning Epilepsy; on the authority of Ibn-Beytár.] ― -b3- SabiY~N also signifies (assumed tropical:) The pupil of the eye: (M, K:) but Kr ascribes this meaning to the vulgar. (M.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) The extremity of each of the jaw-bones: (K, TA:) i. e. (TA) AlS~abiy~aAni signifies the two extremities of the two jaw-bones (S, M, TA) of the camel and of other animals: or, as some say, the two edges curving outwards from the middle of the two jaw-bones: (M, TA:) or, accord. to the A, the thin portions of the two extremities thereof: and it is [said to be] tropical. (TA.) And (assumed tropical:) A bone below the lobe, or lobule, of each of the two ears: (K:) or, as some say, the head of the bone that is below the lobe, or lobule, of each of the two ears by the space of about three fingers put together. (M.) ― -b5- And (tropical:) The edge ( Had~ ) of the sword: (M, K, TA:) or the ridge thereof, (M, TA, in the copies of the K A^awo gayorihi is erroneously put for A^awo Eayoruhu , TA,) which rises in [i. e. along ] its middle; (M, K, TA;) and likewise of a spear-head: (M, TA:) or, accord. to the A, that part of a sword below, or exclusive of, ( duwna ,) its Zubap [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b6- And (assumed tropical:) The head of the human foot; (M, A, TA; in the copies of the K raA^osu Alqawomi is erroneously put for raA^osu Alqadami ; TA;) i. e. the part [thereof] between its HimaArap [q. v.] and the toes. (A, TA.) And AlS~abiy~aAni signifies also (assumed tropical:) The two sides of the [ camel's saddle called ] raHol . (M.) ― -b7- It is also said that SiboyaAnu Aljaliydi signifies (tropical:) The grains of hoar-frost that resemble pearls: and SiboyaAnu AlmaTari (tropical:) the small drops of rain: but accord. to the author of the “ Khasáïl, ” it is Siy^obaAn [pl. of Suw^aAbapN , q. v.], with ' and then b . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: (S, M, A, Msb, K) and ↓ SuforN and ↓ SufurN and ↓ SafirN (M, K) and ↓ SaforN (M) and ↓ A^aSofaru (Msb) Empty, void, or vacant; (S, M, A, Msb, K;) applied to a house or tent, (S, Msb,) and to a vessel, (M, A,) and to a hand: (A:) each of the first three is used alike as masc. and fem. and sing. sourceDefinition: [an inf. n. of Safira , q. v.: ― -b2- and hence,] Hunger: and ↓ SaforapN [the inf. n. un.] a hungering once. (M, K.) ― -b3- Also A certain disease in the belly, which renders the face yellow: (M, K:) or a collecting of water in the belly. (Kt.) [See also SufaArN .] ― -b4- Also A kind of serpent, (S, M, K,) in the belly, (S, K,) which sticks to the ribs, and bites them, (M, K,) or, as the Arabs assert, which bites a man when he is hungry, its bite occasioning the stinging which a man feels when he is hungry: (S:) used alike as sing. and pl.; or one is termed SafarapN : (M:) and it is said to be what is meant by the word in a trad., in which it is disacknowledged: (S, TA:) or a certain reptile ( daAb~ap ) which bites the ribs and their cartilages: (M, K:) or a certain serpent in the belly, which attacks beasts and men, and which, accord. to the Arabs [ of the time of Ignorance ], passes from one to another more than the mange or scab; (Ru-beh:) the Prophet, however, denied its doing so: it is said also that it oppresses and hurts a man when he is hungry: (A'Obeyd:) this is the explanation approved by Az: (TA:) or, as also ↓ SufaArN , worms in the belly, (M, K, TA,) and in the cartilages of the ribs, which cause a man to become very yellow, and sometimes kill him. (TA.) You say, EaD~a EalaY $urosuwfihi AlS~afaru , meaning, (tropical:) He was hungry. (A.) -A2- Accord. to some, (M,) in the trad. above referred to, SafarN signifies The postponing of [ the month ] El-Moharram, transferring it to Safar: (A'Obeyd, M, K:) [see nasiYo'N :] or it there means the disease called by this name, because they asserted it to be transitive. (K.) -A3- Also The intellect, or understanding; or the heart, or mind; syn. ruwEN : (M, K: [in the CK rawoE :]) the inmost part ( lub~ ) of the heart. (M, K.) Hence the saying, (TA,) laA yalotaATu h`*aA biSafariY This will not adhere to me, [or to my mind, ] nor will my soul accept it: (S, TA:) said of that which one does not love. (A.) -A4- Also A contract, compact, or covenant: or suretiship, or responsibility: syn. EaqodN . (M, L, K. [In some copies of the K, fqd .]) -A5- Also (S, M, Msb, K) and sometimes [ Safaru ,] imperfectly decl., (K,) but all make it perfectly decl. except AO, who makes it imperfectly decl. because it is determinate [or a proper name] and similar in meaning to saAEapN , which is fem., meaning that all nouns signifying times are saAEaAt , (Th, M,) and, accord. to some, AlS~afaru , (Msb,) [ The second month of the Arabian calendar; ] the month that is [ the next ] after ElMoharram ( AlmuHar~amu ): (S, M, K:) so called because in it they used to procure their provision of corn from the places [in which it was collected, their granaries having then become empty ( Sifor ); agreeably with the opinion of my learned friend Mons. Fulgence Fresnel, that it was so called from the scarcity of provisions in the season in which it fell when it was first named; for it then fell in winter: see the latter of the two tables in p. 1254; and see also nasiYo'N ]: or because Mekkeh was then empty, its people having gone forth to travel: or, accord. to Ru-beh, because the Arabs in it made predatory expeditions, and left those whom they met empty: (M:) or because they then made predatory expeditions, and left the houses of the people empty: (Msb in art. jmd :) pl. A^aSofaArN , (S, M, Msb, K,) and, as some say, SafaraAtN . (Msb.) ― -b2- AlS~afaraAni The two months of El-Moharram and Safar; (M;) two months of the year, whereof one was called by the Muslims El-Moharram. (IDrd, M, Msb, K.)

sourceDefinition: (S, M, K) and ↓ Safariy~apN (K) The increase, or offspring, ( nitaAj ,) of sheep or goats (S, M, K [in the CK, Aw is erroneously put for w before this explanation]) after that called qayoZiY~N : (S, TA:) or at the period of the [ auroral ] rising of Suheyl [or Canopus, which, in Central Arabia, at the commencement of the era of the Flight, was about the 4th of August, O. S.; here erroneously said in the M to be in the beginning of winter]: (M, K:) or ↓ the latter word signifies [as above, and also the period itself above mentioned: or] the period from the rising of Suheyl to the setting of Al*~iraAE [ the Seventh Mansion of the Moon, which, in the part and age above mentioned, was about the 3rd of January, O. S.], when the cold is intense; and then breeding is approved: (M:) or the period from the rising of Suheyl to the rising of Als~imaAk [ the Fourteenth Mansion of the Moon, which, in the part and age above mentioned, was about the 4th of October, O. S.], commencing with forty nights of varying, or alternating, heat and cold, called AlmuEotadilaAtu : (AZ:) the first increase [of sheep and goats] is the SaqaEiY~ , which is when the sun smites ( taSoqaEu ) the heads of the young ones; and some of the Arabs call it the $amosiY~ , and the qayoZiY~ : then is the SafariY~ , after the SaqaEiY~ ; and that is when the fruit of the palm-tree is cut off: then, the $atawiY~ , which is in the [season called] rabiyE : then, the dafay^iY~ , which is when the sun becomes warm: then, the SayfiY~ : then, the qayoZiY~ : then, the xarafiY~ , in the end of the [season called] qayoZ : (Aboo-Nasr:) or Safariy~apN signifies, (M, K,) and so SafariY~N , (K,) the [ period of the ] departure of the heat and the coming of the cold: (AHn, M, K:) or the period between the departure of the summer and the coming of the winter: (Aboo-Sa'eed:) or the first of the seasons; [app. meaning the autumnal season, called Alxariyf , which was the first of the four, and of the six, seasons; or perhaps the first of the seasons of rain, commonly called AlwasomiY~ ;] and it may be a month: (AHn, M, K:) or the latter, (M,) or both, (TA,) the beginning of the year. (M, TA.) [Hence,] A^ay~aAmu ↓ AlS~afariy~api Twenty days of, or from, ( mino ,) the latter part of the summer, or hot season. (TA voce Hul~abN .) ― -b2- Also the former, (S,) or ↓ both, (TA,) The rain that comes in the beginning of autumn: (S:) or from the period of the rising of Suheyl to that of the setting of Al*~iraAE [expl. above]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also the latter, (S, M,) or ↓ both, (K,) A plant that grows in the beginning of the autumn: (S, M, K:) so called, accord. to AHn, because the beasts become yellow when they pasture upon that which is green; their arm-pits and similar parts, and their lips and fur, becoming yellow; but [ISd says,] I have not found this to be known. (M.)

definition: A sort of dates of El-Yemen, which are dried in the state in which they are termed busor , (AHn, M, K,) being then yellow;
sourceDefinition: A sort of dates of El-Yemen, which are dried in the state in which they are termed busor , (AHn, M, K,) being then yellow; and when they become dry, and are rubbed with the hand, they crumble, and sawiyq is sweetened with them, and they surpass sugar; (AHn, M;) [or] they supply the place of sugar in sawiyq . (K.) -A2- AlS~uforiy~apu , (S, M, K,) and, (K,) or as some say, (S, M,) ↓ AlS~iforiy~apu , (M, K,) A sect of the xawaArij , (S,) a party of the Haruwriy~ap ; (M, K;) so called in relation to Sufrah ( Suforapu [which is the name of a place in El-Yemámeh]): (M:) or in relation to Ziyád Ibn-El-Asfar, (S, K,) their head, or chief; (S;) or to 'Abd-Allah (S, M, K) Ibn-Es-Saffár, (S,) or Ibn-Saffár, (K,) or Ibn-Safár, (so in a copy of the M,) in which case it is extr. in form; (M;) or on account of the yellowness of their complexions; or because of their being void of religion; (K;) accord. to which last derivation, it is ↓ AlS~iforiy~apu , with kesr; and As holds this to be the right opinion. (TA.) ― -b2- And the former ( AlS~uforiy~apu ) The mahaAlibap , (M, K,) who were celebrated for bounty and generosity; (TA;) so called in relation to Aboo-Sufrah, (M, K,) who was [surnamed] Abu-l-Mohelleb. (M.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) like baAEahu , (MF,) [first pers. Sidotu ,] aor. yaSiydu , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. SayodN ; (S, M, Mgh, Msb;) and SaAdahu , (S, &c.,) like haAbahu , (MF,) [first pers. Sidotu , as above, but originally Sayidotu , whereas the first pers. of the former is originally Sayadotu ,] aor. yaSaAdu ; (IAar, S, Msb, K;) and ↓ ASTAdhu , (S, M, A, L, Msb, K,) also written and pronounced AiS~aAdahu ; (L;) and ↓ tSy~dhu ; (M, A, L;) He took, captured, or caught, it; (Mgh, L;) [ made it his prey; ] snared, or ensnared, it; trapped, or entrapped, it; (MF;) or sought to take, capture, catch, snare, or trap, it; hunted it, or chased it: namely, [game, i. e.] any kind of wild animals, or the like, (L,) fowl, &c., (Msb,) and fish. (L.) [And SaAda , and ↓ ASTAd , and ↓ tSy~d , without the mention of the object, this being understood, He took, captured, caught, snared or ensnared, trapped or entrapped, game, i. e. any kind of wild animals, or the like, fowl, &c., or fish; or he sought to take &c.; he hunted or chased, stalked, or lurked for game; he fowled; or he fished. ] You say, ↓ xaraja yataSay~adu [&c., meaning He went forth to take &c., or seeking to take &c., game, or wild animals or the like; to hunt or chase, to stalk, or lurk for game; to fowl; or to fish ]. (S, K.) And AlwaHo$a ↓ xaraja yataSay~adu He went forth [ to take &c., or] seeking to take &c., the wild animals. (L.) And Sidotu fulaAnFA SayodFA i. q. Sidotu lahu [ I took &c., or sought to take &c., for such a one, game, or a wild animal, or wild animals, or the like ]. (M, * K.) And SAd AlmakaAna , and ↓ ASTAdhu , i. q. SAd fiyhi [ He took &c., or sought to take &c., game, or wild animals, or the like, in the place ]: Sb mentions, as a phrase of the Arabs, SidonaA qanawayoni meaning SidonaA waHo$a qanawayoni : qanawaAni being the name of a certain land [or of two mountains]. (M.) And AlS~aqoru yaSiydu [ The hawk preys ]. (Msb and K in art. Sqr .) *awaAtu AlS~ayodi is applied to beasts and to birds [ That prey upon others; predatory ]. (S and K in art. jrj , &c.) ― -b2- [Hence,] one says, huwa yaSiydu Aln~aAsa biAlmaEoruwfi (tropical:) [ He captivates men by goodness, beneficence, or kindness ]. (A.) ― -b3- And AiqotaSido taSido (tropical:) Aim thou at that which is right and just: thou shalt obtain that which thou wantest. (A.) ― -b4- xarajonaA naSiydu bayoDa Aln~aEaAmi (tropical:) [ We went forth to take, or hunt after, the eggs of ostriches ]. (T, TA.) ― -b5- And SidonaA AlkamaA^apa , (M, A, TA,) a good phrase of the Arabs, mentioned, but not expl., by IAar; app. meaning (tropical:) We drew forth truffles [ from the ground ] like as one draws forth wild animals [ from their lurking-places ]. (M, TA.) ― -b6- And SidonaA maA='a Als~amaA='i (tropical:) We took [or caught in vessels or collected ] the water of the sky. (Th, M, A. *) -A2- Sayida , (Lth, S, M, L,) of the dial. of El- Hijáz, aor. yaSoyadu , (Lth, L,) inf. n. SayadN ; (Lth, S, M, L;) and SaAda , (Lth, M, L,) [aor. yaSiydu ;] He (a camel) had the disease termed SayadN [expl. below]: (Lth, S, M, L:) the Y in Sayida is preserved unchanged because it is so preserved in the original form, which is ↓ AiSoyad~a , (S,) though they may not have said AiSoyad~a ; (Sb, M;) and the like is the case in Eawira : (Sb, * S, M: *) the augmentative letters are rejected for the purpose of alleviation: hence, one does not say, in the case of verbs of this class, maA A^afoEalahu , [i. e. maA A^aSoyadahu , and maA A^aEuwarahu , and the like,] forming thus verbs of wonder, because the original form is augmented, and a verb of four letters cannot be formed from a verb of four letters, for a measure can only be formed from a measure that is less. (S.) Also, both verbs, (the former accord. to the S and M, and ↓ the latter likewise accord. to the M,) (assumed tropical:) He (a man) was unable to look aside, (S, M,) by reason of disease. (S.) And Sayida , inf. n. SayadN , (assumed tropical:) He raised his head, by reason of pride: and (assumed tropical:) he (a king) looked not aside, to the right or left. (S.) And Sayida (K, TA, in the CK [erroneously] Say^ida ,) (tropical:) He (a man, TA) had an inclining, or a bending, neck. (K, TA.) -A3- And Sidotu fulaAnFA (tropical:) I made such a one to have an inclining, or a bending, neck. (K, TA. [See also 4.])

definition: , (S, Mgh, * O, Msb, * K,) third pers.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh, * O, Msb, * K,) third pers. Dal~a , (Mgh, Msb,) aor. , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) inf. n. DalaAlN and DalaAlapN ; (S, * O, * Msb;) and Dalilotu , (S, Mgh, * O, Msb, * K,) third pers. as above; (Mgh;) the former of the dial. of Nejd, and the more chaste; the latter of the dial. of the people of El-'Áliyeh, (S, Msb, TA,) and of El- Hijáz, and Kr has mentioned Dililotu for Dalilotu as heard from the tribe of Temeem; (TA;) I erred, strayed, or went astray; (Mgh, Msb;) deviated from the right way or course, or from that which was right; missed, or lost, the right way; or lost my way; DalaAlN and DalaAlapN signifying the contr. of ra$aAdN , (S, O, TA,) and hudFY . (K, TA.) [See DalaAlN below.] Hence, in the Kur [xxxiv. 49], qulo A_ino Dalalotu fiA_in~amaA A^aDil~u EalaY nafosiY [ Say thou, If I err, I shall err only against myself, i. e., to my own hurt]. (O, Msb. [See also x. 108 and xvii. 16 of the Kur.]) One says also, Dal~a DalaAluhu [app. His error became error indeed; a phrase similar to jad~a jid~uhu , q. v.: or his erring passed away; see 4, latter part]. (TA.) And Dal~a Eani AlqaSodi He deviated from the right way or course. (TA.) And the verb is trans. as well as intrans.: you say, Dal~a AlT~ariyqa , and Dal~a Eanohu , aor. and , (Mgh, Msb,) inf. ns. as above, meaning He erred, strayed, or went astray, from the road, or way; (Msb;) he did not find the way to the road: (Mgh, Msb:) and of anything stationary, if you miss the place thereof, you say Dalalotuhu and Dalilotuhu : (Az, Msb:) or you say, Dalilotu AlT~ariyqa , (K,) or Dalilotu Almasojida , and Ald~aAra , (ISk, S, O,) [ I missed, or lost, the right way to the road, or the mosque, and the house, ] when you know not the place thereof: (ISk, S, O:) and in like manner, anything stationary, to which one does not find the way: (ISk, S, O, K:) and AA says the like: but that one says of a thing that falls from his hand, and a thing that quits its place, ↓ A^aDolalotuhu , (IB, TA,) which means I lost it, and knew not its place; meaning, for instance, a horse, or she-camel, or the like: (Az, Msb:) [thus] one says, A^aDolalotu biEiyriY [ I lost my camel, and knew not his place, ] (AA, ISk, S, IB, O) when his shank has been tied up to his arm and one does not find the way to him, and when he has been left loose and has gone away whither one knows not: (AA, IB, TA:) but Yoo differs from others respecting this case; for, accord. to him, one says, ADl~ fulaAnN baEiyrahu and also Dal~ahu , in the same sense; (O, TA;) and the like is said in the K: (TA:) and it is also said in the Bári' that when you seek an animal and miss its place and find not the way to it, it is regarded as in the category of stationary things, and therefore you say Dalilotuhu . (Msb.) ― -b2- Dal~a signifies also He was, or became, confounded, or perplexed, and unable to see his right course. (Ibn-Es-Seed, TA.) ― -b3- Also, aor. (S, O, K) and , (K,) the pret. being like zal~a and mal~a , (TA,) inf. n. DalaAl , It (a thing, S, O, TA) became lost; [as though it went astray;] it perished, came to nought, or passed away. (S, O, K, TA.) Thus in the phrase Dal~a Ean~iY ka*aA Such a thing became lost from me. (Mgh.) One says to him from whom pieces of money have dropped, qado Dal~ato Eanoka [ They have become lost from thee ]. (TA.) And to him who has done a deed from which no profit has resulted, you say, qad Dal~a saEoyuka (tropical:) [ Thy labour has been lost ]: the like occurs in the Kur xviii. 104, meaning DaAEa . (TA, in two places.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) He (a man, TA) died, and became dust and bones. (K, TA.) In this sense the verb is used in the Kur xxxii. 9: but some there read, in the place of DalalonaA , SalilonaA [q. v.], with S : (TA:) or the verb in that instance has the meaning here next following. (S.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) He, or it, (a man, S, TA, or a camel, Msb, and a thing, TA,) was, or became, unperceived or imperceptible, unapparent, latent, hidden or concealed, or absent, (S, Msb, K, TA.) Hence the phrase, Dal~a AlmaA='u fiY All~abani (tropical:) [ The water became unperceived, or concealed, in the milk ]. (TA.) One says of a road to which he has not been able to find the way, Dal~a Ean~iY [ It has become hidden from me ]. (K, TA.) And hence also the saying of a man, as is related in a trad., (S, O, TA,) after his having charged his sons by saying to them, “ When I die, burn ye me; and when I shall have become ashes, pound me; then scatter me in the water: ” (O, TA:) laEal~iY A^aDil~u A@ll~`h (S, O, TA) i. e. (assumed tropical:) May-be, I shall be unperceived by God, or concealed from Him: (S:) or may-be, I shall be hidden, or absent, from God's punishment: (O, TA:) or, as El-'Otbee says, may-be, I shall escape God, and my place will be hidden from Him. (TA.) And Dal~a said of one forgetting means (assumed tropical:) His memory became absent from him. (O, Msb, TA.) A^ano taDil~a A_iHodaAhumaA , or A_ino taDil~a , in the Kur [ii. 282], accord. to different readers, (TA,) in which instance A^ano and A_ino are syn., (Mughnee, [see A^ano , in p. 106, cols. 1 and 2,]) means If one of them twain [referring to women] be absent from her memory: or if the memory of one of them twain be absent from her: [or if one of them twain err in her memory: ] or, accord. to Zj, the meaning of the verb in this case is that which next follows. (TA.) ― -b6- Dalilotu Al$~aYo'a also signifies (assumed tropical:) I forgot the thing: whence one says of a woman, Dal~ato A^ay~aAma HayoDihaA (assumed tropical:) [ She forgot the days of her menstruation ]; and so ↓ A^aDal~atohaA : (Mgh:) or Dal~a fulaAnFA (assumed tropical:) He was made, or caused, to forget such a one. (K. [In the CK, Aunosiyohi is erroneously put for A^unosiyahu .]) It is said that laA yaDil~u rab~iY , in the Kur xx. 54, means (assumed tropical:) My Lord will not be unmindful: or nothing will escape Him. (TA.) ― -b7- And one says, Dal~aniY fulaAnN , (Msb, K,) or Dal~aniY fulaAnN falamo A^aqodaro Ealayohi , (O,) meaning Such a one went away from me, (O, Msb, K,) and I was unable to compass him [or to find him ]: so in the Bári'. (Msb.) -A2- Dul~a , as a verb of wonder: see Dul~N .

And hence also the saying of a man, as is related in a trad., (S, O, TA,) after his having charged his sons by saying to them, “ When I die, burn ye me; and when I shall have become ashes, pound me; then scatter me in the water: ” (O, TA:) laEal~iY A^aDil~u A@ll~`h (S, O, TA) i. e. (assumed tropical:) May-be, I shall be unperceived by God, or concealed from Him: (S:) or may-be, I shall be hidden, or absent, from God's punishment: (O, TA:) or, as El-'Otbee says, may-be, I shall escape God, and my place will be hidden from Him. (TA.) And Dal~a said of one forgetting means (assumed tropical:) His memory became absent from him. (O, Msb, TA.) A^ano taDil~a A_iHodaAhumaA , or A_ino taDil~a , in the Kur [ii. 282], accord. to different readers, (TA,) in which instance A^ano and A_ino are syn., (Mughnee, [see A^ano , in p. 106, cols. 1 and 2,]) means If one of them twain [referring to women] be absent from her memory: or if the memory of one of them twain be absent from her: [or if one of them twain err in her memory: ] or, accord. to Zj, the meaning of the verb in this case is that which next follows. (TA.) ― -b6- Dalilotu Al$~aYo'a also signifies (assumed tropical:) I forgot the thing: whence one says of a woman, Dal~ato A^ay~aAma HayoDihaA (assumed tropical:) [ She forgot the days of her menstruation ]; and so ↓ A^aDal~atohaA : (Mgh:) or Dal~a fulaAnFA (assumed tropical:) He was made, or caused, to forget such a one. (K. [In the CK, Aunosiyohi is erroneously put for A^unosiyahu .]) It is said that laA yaDil~u rab~iY , in the Kur xx. 54, means (assumed tropical:) My Lord will not be unmindful: or nothing will escape Him. (TA.) ― -b7- And one says, Dal~aniY fulaAnN , (Msb, K,) or Dal~aniY fulaAnN falamo A^aqodaro Ealayohi , (O,) meaning Such a one went away from me, (O, Msb, K,) and I was unable to compass him [or to find him ]: so in the Bári'. (Msb.) -A2- Dul~a , as a verb of wonder: see Dul~N .

definition: , inf. n. A_iDolaAlN , He, or it, made him, or caused him, to err, stray, or go astray; to deviate from the right way or course, or from that which was right; to miss, or lose, the right way; or to...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. A_iDolaAlN , He, or it, made him, or caused him, to err, stray, or go astray; to deviate from the right way or course, or from that which was right; to miss, or lose, the right way; or to lose his way. (Az, TA.) [See also 2, first sentence.] AlA_iDolaAlu is of two sorts: one of these is the consequence of erring, or straying; either as in the case in which one says A^aDolalotu AlbaEiyra (expl. above, see 1, former half); or the decreeing that one shall err, or stray, &c., because he has done so already, and this is sometimes the case when the A_iDolaAl of a man is attributed to God: the other sort is the embellishing [or commending] to a man that which is false, or wrong, or vain, in order that he may err, or stray, &c.: and God's A_iDolaAl of a man is of two sorts; one of which has been expl. above; the other is God's so constituting man that when he observes [and pursues] a certain course, or way, [of acting or the like], whether it be such as is commended or such as is discommended, he habituates himself to it, and esteems it pleasant, and keeps to it, and finds it difficult to turn from it, wherefore it is said that custom is a second nature. (Er-Rághib, TA.) ― -b2- Also He, or it, made, or caused, him, or it, to perish, or become lost; syn. A^aholakahu , (S, TA,) and A^aDaAEahu , (El-Fárábee, S, O, Msb,) or Day~aEahu ; (TA;) [ ADAEhu and Dy~Ehu signifying the same; and so ADl~hu and ↓ Dll~`hu ; whence,] A^alamo yajoEalo kayodahumo fiY taDoliylK , in the Kur cv. 2, means [ Did He not make their plot to be such as ended] in a causing to perish, or become lost, ( fiY taDoyiyEK ,) and in annulment? (Ksh, Bd.) A^aDal~a A^aEomaAlahumo , in the Kur [xlvii. 1 and 9, which may be rendered (assumed tropical:) He will cause their works to be lost, or to be of no effect ], means, accord. to Aboo-Is-hák, He will not recompense them for their good works; the phrase being similar to the saying qado Dal~a saEoyuka [expl. above]. (TA.) And A^aDal~a A@ll~`hu DalaAlaka (assumed tropical:) [ May God make thine erring to be no more, or to come to an end, ] is expl. by ISk as meaning may thine erring pass away from thee, so that thou shalt not err; and he adds that the saying mal~a malaAluka means *ahaba Eanoka Hat~aY laA tamal~a . (TA.) ― -b3- Also (tropical:) He buried, and hid, or concealed, him, or it. (K, TA.) You say, A^uDil~a Almay~itu (tropical:) The dead was buried. (S, O.) The phrase A^aDal~ato bihi A^um~uhu , meaning (tropical:) His mother buried him, in a verse cited by IAar, is extr., or anomalous. (TA.) ― -b4- And He found him to be erring, straying, going astray; deviating from the right way or course, or from that which was right; missing, or losing, the right way; losing his way; not rightly directed, or not finding the way to the truth: like as one says A^aHomadahu , and A^aboxalahu . (TA.) ― -b5- And you say, A^aDal~aniY ka*aA , meaning (assumed tropical:) Such a thing was, or became, beyond my power, or compass. (IAar, Msb, TA.) ― -b6- See also 1, near the end.

sourceDefinition: : see DalaAlN . ― -b2- [Also, app. as meaning A lost state; a state of perishing, coming to nought, or passing away; ] a subst. from Dal~a signifying DaAEa and halaka . (S, TA.) ― -b3- And hence [its usage, in the manner of a proper name, in] the saying, huwa Dul~u bonu Dul~K , (S,) which means, (S, O, K,) as also ↓ huwa Dil~u bonu Dil~K , (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K,) He is the unknown, the son of the unknown; (S, Z, O, K;) and in like manner, bonu Alt~alaAli ↓ AlD~alaAlu ; (S, O;) and qul~u bonu qul~K : (TA:) or he is one in whom is no good: (K:) or he is one who persists in error. (M, K.) ― -b4- [Hence also, perhaps, it is said that] yaA Dul~a maA tajoriY bihi AlEaSaA [in the CK Dal~a ] means yaA faqodahu and yaA talafahu [i. e., app., O the loss, or O the coming to nought, of that by reason of which the mare El-'Asà is running! ]: (K, TA:) a prov.; said by Kaseer Ibn-Saad to Jedheemeh El-Abrash, when he went with him to Ez-Zebbà; for when they were within her province, he repented, and Kaseer said to him, “ Mount this my horse, and escape upon him, for his dust will not be cloven [by the pursuer, ” i. e. he will not be overtaken]: (TA: [but the mare is thus made a male:]) or it was said by 'Amr Ibn-'Adee, when he saw El-'Asà, the mare of Jedheemeh, with Kaseer upon her: qawomu is suppressed after yA ; and ↓ Dul~a is of the forms [of verbs] denoting wonder, originally Dalula , with damm, like Hub~a in the phrase Hub~a bifulaAnK , originally Habuba ; and the meaning of the prov. is, O people, what a case of perdition is that by reason of which El-'Asà is running! i. e., the death of Jedheemeh. (Meyd.) ― -b5- Dul~N bitaDolaAlK [in CK Dal~N ] means A vain, or futile, thing: (S, O, K:) [or a vain, misleading thing; taDolaAlN being an inf. n. of Dal~ala :] 'Amr Ibn-Shás El-Asadee says, ta*ak~arotu layolaY laAta Hiyna A@dikaArihaA waqado HuniYa AlA^aDolaAEu Dul~N bitaDolaAli [ I remembered Leylà when it was not a time for remembering her, the ribs having become bent by the bending of the back with age: it was a vain, misleading thing ]. (S, O.) ― -b6- Dul~u A^aDolaAlK : see Dil~apN .

sourceDefinition: [an inf. n. of 1: used as a simple subst.,] Error; contr. of ra$aAdN , (S, O, TA,) and of hudFY ; (K, TA;) as also ↓ DalaAlapN , (S, O, K,) and ↓ Dal~N , and ↓ Dul~N , and ↓ Dil~apN , and ↓ DalalN , and ↓ DaloDalapN , (K,) and ↓ DulaDilapN , (O, TA,) and ↓ A^uDoluwlapN , (K,) of which last the pl. is A^aDaAliylu , (Lth, O, TA,) as in the saying tamaAdaY fiY A^aDaAliyli AlhawaY [ He persevered in the errors of love ], (TA,) or A^aDaAliylu , as some say, has no sing., or its sing. is supposed, or has been heard, and is A^uDoluwlapN or A^uDoluwlN or A_iDoliylN or some other form: (MF, TA:) the primary signification of AlD~alaAlu is the going away from the right course, or direction: (Ham p. 357:) or it signifies, accord. to Ibn-El-Kemál, the loss, or missing, of that which brings, or conducts, to the object sought: or, as some say, the pursuing a way that will not bring, or conduct, to that object: or, accord. to Er-Rághib, the deviating from the right way: and it is said to be any deviation from that which is right, intentional or unintentional, little or much; because the right and approved way is very difficult; wherefore it may be used of him who commits any mistake whatever, and is imputed to prophets and to unbelievers, though between the DlAl of the former and that of the latter is a wide difference: and in another point of view, it is of two sorts; one is in the speculative departments of knowledge, as in acquaintance with the unity of God, and with the prophetic function or office, and the like, indicated in the Kur iv. 135; or it is in the practical departments of knowledge, as in acquaintance with the ordinances of the law, that is, religious services. (TA.) ― -b2- Also A state of perdition: so in the Kur liv. 24: (S, O:) [and in like manner ↓ DalaAlapN ; for] DalaAlapu AlEamali signifies The annulled and lost state of work. (TA.) ― -b3- And Absence, or a state of concealment. (Msb. [This is there said to be the primary signification.]) ― -b4- huwa AlD~alaAlu bonu Alt~alaAli see expl. voce Dul~N .

definition: A man (S, O) who errs, strays, goes astray, or deviates from the right way or course, much, or often: (S, O, K:) or (tropical:) who errs, &c.
sourceDefinition: A man (S, O) who errs, strays, goes astray, or deviates from the right way or course, much, or often: (S, O, K:) or (tropical:) who errs, &c., much, or often, in religion: (TA:) and ↓ muDal~alN , (S, TA,) which in some of the copies of the S is written thus and also muDal~il , (TA,) signifies the same; (S, TA;) or one who is not disposed, or directed, to good; in the K, Al~*Y lA yuwaf~iY bixayorK , [or yuwfiY bxyr , as in the CK,] but correctly Al~*Y lA yuwaf~aqu lixayorK ; or, as some say, a committer of errors, and of false, wrong, or vain, actions: and Dil~iylN is also expl. as signifying one who will not desist from error. definition: a word imitative of a sound;
sourceDefinition: a word imitative of a sound; and sometimes they said ↓ TaqoTaqapN : (IDrd, O, TA:) or the former is a word imitative of The sound of stones; and ↓ the latter is its noun: (K:) one says, AlHijaArapi ↓ samiEotu TaqoTaqapa I heard [ the sound of ] the falling of the stones, one upon another, when they rolled down from a mountain: (IDrd, O:) or Taqo is a word imitative of the sound of the stone and of the solid hoof; and ↓ TaqoTaqapN signifies the action thereof: (M, TA:) or this latter is a word imitative of the sound of the successive falling of stones, one upon another: (IDrd, O:) or this word signifies the sound of the legs of horses upon the hard ground; (IAar, TA;) [or] sometimes it signifies also the sound of the solid hoofs upon the ground; (IDrd, O;) or the sounds of the hoofs of horses or similar beasts [ with quick reiteration ]; like daqodaqapN ; and sometimes they said ↓ HabaTiqoTiqo , of which El-Mázinee cites an ex.; (S, O;) but [J says] I have not seen this except in his book: (S:) another ex. of it, however, is cited by Lth. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: The sea: (S, K, TA:) said to be so called because of its overwhelming what is in it ( liA^an~ahu Tam~a EalaY maA fiyhi ): but in this sense the word is said to be ↓ Tam~N , and to be pronounced with kesr for the purpose of assimilating it to rim~N . (TA.) One says, jaA='a biAlT~im~i waAlr~im~i , meaning He brought much wealth: (S, TA:) or the meaning in this instance is AlAmr Alkvyr [app. a mistranscription for AlA^amor Alkabiyr i. e. that which was a great event ]: so says As: or much of everything: or much and little: thus accord. to Aboo-Tálib: or what was moist and what was dry: or the leaves of trees, and what had fallen off from them. (TA. [See more voce rim : and see also what here follows.]) ― -b2- And Water: (K, TA:) or much water; as also ↓ TaAm~N [or maA='N TaAm~N ]: (TA:) or the rubbish and scum, and the like, that is upon its surface; or that is driven along by it: (K, * TA:) and thus expl. as used in the saying above-mentioned. (TA.) ― -b3- And A large number: (K:) and this also is said to be meant in the phrase above. (TA.) ― -b4- And A wonderful thing; syn. EajabN and EajiybN [which here, as in many other instances, evidently signify the same]: (K:) and this too is said to be meant in the phrase above. (TA.) ― -b5- And A male ostrich: (K:) because of the lightness of his pace. (TA.) ― -b6- And A courser, or swift horse; as also ↓ TamiymN : (K, * TA: [see also TamuwmN :]) called Tim~N because of. his light and quick, or easy, running ( liTamiymi Eadowihi ); or as being likened to the sea, as a horse is termed baHorN and sakobN and garobN . (TA.) ― -b7- And A large *akar : (K:) because its head is maTomuwm [as though this epithet meant “ bare ”]. (TA.) ― -b8- AlT~im~u is also said in the K to signify Alkay~isu ; but [SM says] I think that this is a mistranscription for AlT~am~u meaning Alkabosu [see Tam~a Alr~akiy~apa , in the first paragraph]. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ TumoTumaAniY~N (S, K) and ↓ TimoTimiY~N (K) and ↓ TumaATimN (TA) A man having a barbarousness, or vitiousness, or an impotence, or impediment, in his speech, or utterance, not speaking clearly,...
sourceDefinition: and ↓ TumoTumaAniY~N (S, K) and ↓ TimoTimiY~N (K) and ↓ TumaATimN (TA) A man having a barbarousness, or vitiousness, or an impotence, or impediment, in his speech, or utterance, not speaking clearly, or correctly: (S, K, TA:) and Aboo-Turáb explains [the pl. of the first] TamaATimu as meaning foreigners ( Eajam ). (TA.) Hence the saying of the poet, (S,) 'Antarah, (TA,) taA^owiY lahu quluSu Aln~aEaAmi kamaA A^awato xiraqN yamaAniy~apN liA^aEojama TimoTimi (S, TA;) respecting which Fr relates his having heard El-Mufaddal say that one of the most learned of men explained to him Alxiraqu AlyamaAniy~apu as meaning the clouds [app. likened to rags of cloth of El-Yemen], and AlA^aEojamu AlTimoTimu as meaning the sound of thunder: (TA:) or the latter hemistich is thus: HizaqN yamaAniy~apN liA^aEojama TimoTimi and the verse means, To whom (referring to a male ostrich) repair the young ostriches, like as herds of camels of El-Yemen repair to one who is impotent, and indistinct, or incorrect, in speech: he likens the male ostrich, in respect of blackness, and want of speech, to an Abyssinian pastor impotent, and indistinct, or incorrect, in speech. (EM p. 231.) ― -b2- TimoTimN signifies also A sort of sheep, haring small ears, and A^agobaAb [or what resemble dewlaps ], like the AgbAb of oxen: they are in the region of El-Yemen. (IDrd, TA.)

sourceDefinition: is the inf. n. of 1 [q. v.]: and [it is said that it] signifies The withering, or drying up, of the lip, from thirst: (M:) so says Lth: but it signifies paucity of the flesh and blood of the lip; not the withering, or drying-up, in consequence of thirst: it is a quality that is commended: (T:) or a tawny, or brownish, or dusky, colour, and a withering, or drying-up, in the lip. (S.) ― -b2- And Paucity of the blood of the gum: (Lth, T:) or paucity of the blood and flesh of the gum. (M.) (T.)

definition: Anything withering, or withered;
sourceDefinition: Anything withering, or withered; or becoming, or become, dried up; from heat; as also ↓ ZamK . (M.) ― -b2- [Hence,] $afapN ZamoyaA='u A lip that is not swollen, [ not ] having much blood; (T;) accord. to Lth, from thirst; but AZ says that it is not so: (TA: [see ZamFY :]) or a lip in which is a tawny, or brownish, or dusky, colour, and a withering, or lack of moisture: (S:) or a lip withering, or withered, or lacking moisture, inclining to a tawny, or brownish, or dusky, colour. (K.) ― -b3- And livapN ZamoyaA='u A gum having little blood: (S, K:) or, accord. to the M, having little blood and flesh. (TA.) ― -b4- And EayonN ZamoyaA='u An eye having a thin, or delicate, lid: (T, S, M, K:) and so Eyn ZamoA^aY . (M and TA in art. ZmA^ .) ― -b5- And saAqN ZamoyaA='u A lean shank: (S, M, K:) and so sAq ZamoA^aY . (T and TA in art. ZmA^ .) And A^aZomaY Al$~awaY means A horse having little flesh upon the legs: (TA:) and so ZamoA=nu Al$~awaY . (T in art. rwY .) ― -b6- A^aZomaY is also applied to a man, as signifying Black in the lip: (M:) and so ZamoyaA='u applied to a woman. (T, M.) ― -b7- And the former applied to a man, and the latter to a woman, Having the quality of the gum termed ZamFY expl. above. (M.) ― -b8- Both also, accord. to Lh, signify Tawny, brownish, or dusky; the former as applied to a man, and the latter to a woman: (M:) and thus the former applied to a spear, (As, T, S, M,) and the latter to a spearshaft ( qanaAp ). (TA.) ― -b9- And A^aZomaY signifies also Black: (T:) thus as applied to shade: (S:) and so the fem. applied to a she-camel: (K:) or the latter applied to a she-camel, and [the pl.] ZumoYN applied to camels, in the colour of which is a blackness. (T.) [See also A^aZomaA^u , in art. ZmA^ .]

definition: and ↓ EatomN signify The being slow, or tardy.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ EatomN signify The being slow, or tardy. (S.) You say, Et~m qiraAhu and ↓ Eatama His entertainment for his guest, or guests, was, or became, slow, or tardy; syn. A^aboTaA^a [not A^aboTaA^a bihi ]: (S, K:) and he delayed it: (TA: [but this, though virtually a correct rendering, is app. not so literally:]) and ↓ AEtm likewise has the former meaning: (K:) or qiraY AlDayofi ↓ AEtm signifies he delayed the entertainment of the guest. (S.) And maA Eat~ama A^ano faEala ka*aA He delayed not, or was not slow, to do, or in doing, such a thing. (S, K. *) And HaAjatahu ↓ AEtm He delayed [ the accomplishment of ] the object of his want. (TA.) ― -b2- And Et~m Eanohu He refrained, forbore, abstained, or desisted, from it, (S, K,) namely, an affair, (S,) after having made progress therein; as also ↓ AEtm ; and ↓ Eatama , aor. , (K, TA,) inf. n. EatomN : (TA:) or this last signifies he withheld himself from doing it, meaning, a thing that he desired: (K:) and ↓ AEtm signifies he delayed to do it. (TA.) And [hence] one says, Darabahu famaA Eat~ama , (S,) and Hamala Ealayohi fama Eat~ama , (S, K,) i. e. [ He beat him, and he attacked him, ] and did not withhold, or restrict, or limit, himself, in beating him, [and in attacking him, ] (S,) or and did not recede, or draw back, or desist: (K, TA:) the vulgar say, Darabahu famaA Eat~aba . (S.) ― -b3- See also 4.

definition: Slowness, or tardiness: (IB, TA:) hence the saying of a rájiz, bi*iY salamo TayofN A^alamo bayona Alxayamo ↓ yasoriY Eatamo meaning yasoriY baTiyoy^FA , [i.
sourceDefinition: Slowness, or tardiness: (IB, TA:) hence the saying of a rájiz, bi*iY salamo TayofN A^alamo bayona Alxayamo ↓ yasoriY Eatamo meaning yasoriY baTiyoy^FA , [i. e. A phantom visited ( A^alamo being for A^alam~a ) in Dhoo-Selem, journeying by night slowly amid the tents, ] the p of Eatamap [i. e. EatamapF ] being elided. (TA. [But EatamN is also mentioned in the TA, in the beginning of this art., not as being originally EatamapN , but simply as a subst. in the sense expl. above.]) -A2- [Also, in its most usual sense,] The first third of the night, after the disappearance of the $afaq [or redness that is seen in the sky after sunset ]; (Kh, S, Msb, K;) the first part of the night, after the setting of the light of the $afaq : (Msb:) or the time of the prayer of nightfall: (S, K:) but the calling of that prayer the prayer of the Eatamap , as the Arabs of the desert called it, instead of calling it the prayer of the Ei$aA=' , is said to be forbidden in a trad. (TA.) ― -b2- Eatamapu rubaEK [ The Etmp of a young camel brought forth in the rabiyE , which is the beginning of the breeding-time ], (S, K,) meaning the space during which it (i. e. the rubaE ) is confined at its evening-feed, (K,) is applied to the moonlight of the night when the moon is four nights old. (S, K.) AZ says, The Arabs say in relation to the moon when it is one night old, Eatamapu suxayolapK Hal~a A^aholuhaA birumayolapK [ The Etmp of a little lamb or kid, the owners of which have alighted in a small tract of sand ]; meaning that it does not long continue; like the lamb, or kid, that sucks its mother and soon returns to the sucking: and when it is two nights old, Hadiyvu A^amatayoni bika*ibK wamayonK [ The discourse of two female slaves, with lying and falsehood ]; because their discourse is not long, by reason of their being busied with the serving of their owners: and when it is three nights old, Hadiyvu fatayaAtK gayori muw^otalifaAtK [ The discourse of young women not united by affection ]: and when it is four nights old, Eatamapu rubaEK gayori jaAy^iEK walaA muroDaEK [ The Etmp of a rbE (expl. above) not hungry nor suckled ]; meaning that it is limited to the space of the fuwaAq [or time between two suckings] of this rbE or of the fwAq [or time between two milkings] of its mother; or, as IAar says, Eatamapu A^um~i Alr~ubaEi [ The Etmp of the mother of the rbE ]: and when it is five nights old, HadiyvN waA^unosN wabaqaA='u Ea$aA='i xalifaAtK quEosK [ Discourse and sociableness, and the continuance of the evening-feed of pregnant camels having their heads and necks inclining towards their backs: see also art. qEs ]: and when it is six nights old, yasorN wabat~N [app. A twisting and a grinding by a turning towards the left and from the left; as though meaning that it is a time fit for active employment]: and when it is seven nights old, dulojapu AlD~abuEi [ The night-journeying of the hyena ]: and when it is eight nights old, qamarN A_iDoHiyaAnN [ A bright moon ]: and when it is nine nights old, yuloqaTu fiyhi AljazoEu [ The onyx is picked up in it, being distinguishable by the light of the moon]: and when it is ten nights old, muxan~iqu Alfajori [lit. The choker of the dawn; as though its light were about to overtake, and grapple with, that of daybreak]. (TA.) [It should be observed that every one of these ten sayings is fancifully framed so as to rhyme, perfectly or imperfectly, with words preceding it: the first being preceded by Aibonu layolapK ; the second, by Aibonu layolatayoni ; the third, by Aibonu valaAvK ; the fourth, by Aibonu A^arobaEK ; and so on.] ― -b3- EatamapN signifies also The darkness of the night: (S, K, TA:) or the darkness of the first part of the night, [ after nightfall, i. e.] after the setting of the light of the $afaq [or redness that is seen in the sky after sunset ]: and the vulgar [sometimes] pronounce it Eatomap . (TA.) ― -b4- And The remains of the milk that has collected in the udders of the camels, or of the camels and other cattle, at the period thus termed. (S, ISd, K.) One says, HalabonaA EatamapF [ We milked some remains of what had collected in the udders &c.]. (S, TA.) And Hulibato EatamatuhaA The milk that was obtained from them at the period termed the Eatamap was drawn. (TA, from the trad. of Aboo-Dharr.) And qaEada EinodanaA fulaAnN qadora Eatamapi AlHalaAy^ibi i. e. [ Such a one sat with us, or at our abode, ] as long as the space during which the milch camels are confined for the purpose of the collecting of the milk in their udders. (Har p. 127.)

sourceDefinition: a subst. from Ead~ahu “ he numbered it; ” as also ↓ EadiydN : (S, O, K:) [originally] What is numbered, counted, reckoned, or computed: (O, Msb, K: [in the CK, a w is inadvertently omitted after the explanation of this meaning:]) [and hence,] a number; (Msb;) and ↓ EadiydN is syn. therewith [in this sense, as will be seen in what follows]; (A;) a quantity composed of units; and therefore not [properly] applicable to one; but accord. to the grammarians, one belongs to the predicament of AlEadadu because it is the root thereof, and because it implies quantity, for when it is said “ How many hast thou? ” it is as proper to answer “ One ” as it is to answer “ Three ” &c.: (Msb:) pl. A^aEodaAdN . (TA.) ↓ maA A^akovara Eadiydahumo means Eadadahumo [i. e. How great is their number! ]. (A.) Zj says that EadadN is sometimes used in the sense of an inf. n.; as in the phrase in the Kur [xviii. 10], siniyna EadadFA : but many say that it is in this instance used in its proper sense, meaning maEoduwdapF [i. e. numbered ], and is made masc. because siniyn is syn. with A^aEowaAm . (Msb.) In the phrase waA^aHoSaY kul~a $aYo'K EadadFA , in the Kur [lxxii. last verse], it is used in its proper sense of maEoduwdFA , and is put in the accus. case as a denotative of state; or it is used in this case as an inf. n. (IAth, O.) ― -b2- It signifies also The years of a man's life, which one numbers, or counts. (IAar, O, K. [In the CK, after the words waAlEadadu AlmEduwdu , a w should be inserted.]) Hence the phrase raq~a Eadaduhu The years of his life, which he numbered, became few, the greater part having passed. (IAar, O.)

sourceDefinition: an inf. n. of 3 [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b2- yawomu AlEidaAdi [as expl. by Sh: see 3, first sentence. ― -b3- Also] The day of giving: (S, O:) AlEidaAd signifies AlEaTaA=' (S, O, K) in this phrase. (S, O.) ― -b4- And i. q. yawomu AlEaroDi [which generally means The day of the last judgment ]. (TA.) ― -b5- And one says, A^atayotu fulaAnFA fiY yawomi EidaAdK meaning I came to such a one on a Friday ( ywm HumuEapK ), or on a Minor Festival ( ywm fiTorK ), or on a Great Festival ( ywm A^aDoHaY ). (O, K, * TA.) ― -b6- And laqiytu fulaAnFA EidaAda Alv~uray~aA , (S, O, K,) or EidaAda Alv~uray~aA Alqamara , and fiY nuzuwli Alqamari Alv~uray~aA , (TA,) meaning I met such a one once in the month: (S, O, K:) because the moon makes its abode in Alvry~A [the Pleiades, its third Mansion,] once in every month: (S, O:) IB [understood the meaning to be, once in the year; for he] asserts that, correctly, J should have said, because the moon is in conjunction with Alvry~A once in every year, and that is on the fifth day of [the Syrian month] Ádhár [corresponding to March O. S.], agreeably with what is said in a verse of Ibn-Holáhil which will be found cited in what follows: but [this verse evidently relates to what was the case in its author's time; for it is well known that] the moon traverses the firmament once in every month, and is every night in a [different], Mansion, and it is therefore in [the Mansion of] Alvry~A once in every month. (L, TA.) [Accord. to some,] one says, laA A=tiyka A_il~aA EidaAda Alqamari Alv~uray~aA , meaning I will not come to thee save once in the year: because the moon makes its abode in Alvry~A but once in the year: (A:) and maA yaA^otiynaA fulaAnN A_il~aA EidaAda Alv~uray~aA Alqamara , and A_il~aA qiraAna Alqamari Alv~uray~aA , meaning Such a one comes not to us save once in the year: and maA A^aloqaAhu A_il~aA Alv~uray~aA Alqamara ↓ Eid~apa , and Al~A EidaAda Alv~uray~aA Alqamara , and Al~A EidaAda Alv~uray~aA mina Alqamari , meaning I do not meet him save once in the year: (TA:) [but these explanations are probably founded upon a want of due consideration of a statement which here follows:] after citing this verse of Aseed, or Useyd, or Useiyid, [written in the TA Asyd ,] Ibn-Holáhil, or Ibn-El-Holáhil, [thus differently written in different places,] A_i*aA maA qaArana Alqamaru Alv~uray~aA livaAlivapi faqado *ahaba Al$~itaA='u [ When the moon is in conjunction with the Pleiades in a third night, then winter has departed ], AHeyth said, [as though what was the case at a particular period of a cycle were the case generally,] the moon is in conjunction with Alvry~A only in a third night from the new moon, [meaning only once in the year in the third night,] and that is in the beginning of spring and the end of winter. (TA.) ― -b7- And EidaAdN and ↓ EidadN , (S, O, K,) the latter a contraction of the former, used by poetic license, (S, O,) signify A paroxysm of pain which a person stung or bitten by a venomous reptile suffers on the completion of a year from the day on which he was stung or bitten: (S, O, K: *) a paroxysm of pain occurring at a certain period: (A:) a paroxysm such as that of a tertian, or quartan, fever; and the pain of poison which kills at a certain period: and the regular period of the return of a fever is called its EidaAd . (TA.) One says, A^atatohu All~asoEapu liEidaAdK The pain of the venomous sting, or bite, returned to him with vehemence at the expiration of a year. (S, O, * K.) And bihi maraDN EidaAdN He has a malady that intermits and returns. (A.) And EidaAdu Als~aliymi is said to signify A period of seven days from that on which the person has received a venomous sting or bite: when it has expired, his recovery is hoped for: as long as it has not expired, one says, huwa fiY EidaAdihi . (A, TA.) [See also 3.] ― -b8- EidaAdN signifies also The time of death. (O, K.) ― -b9- And A day, or night, when the family of a person deceased assemble together to wail for him. (ISk, TA.) ― -b10- And A touch of insanity or diabolical possession: (S, O, K:) or an affection resembling insanity or diabolical possession, that takes a man at certain times. (Az, TA.) One says, biAlr~ajuli EidaAdN In the man is a touch of insanity [&c.]. (S, O.) ― -b11- And The twanging of a bow; (S, O, K; *) and so ↓ EadiydN . (O, K.) ― -b12- See also the next paragraph, in five places: ― -b13- and see EadiydapN .
